REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1       The Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of the heavy engineering industry,
machine tool industry, heavy electrical industry, industrial machinery and auto-industry. The Industries covered by this
Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport.
They also cater to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers,
refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for development of
a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
It is  also  vested with the administrative charge of 48 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).
 
1.2       The  PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of
engineering/capital goods, consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 48 Public Sector
Enterprises under the Department was about Rs.7780.24 crores  till  March, 2000  employing about 1.61 lakh  persons.
 
1.3       The Department holds interactions with various industry councils and evolves plans for their growth. The
Department also assists Public Sector Enterprises through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and
trade, technological collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

2.4          It was also stated that the performance of  PSEs has been below the projected levels primarily due to the
shortage of orders and working capital, high cost of production, inability to face competition and excessive manpower. 
In order to overcome these constraints, concerted efforts have been made including restructuring of PSEs.  The
Government have approved reservation of orders for HCL from DOT/MTNL.  Ministry of Railways has been persuaded
to increase the volume of orders for wagons placed on the BBUNL group of companies.  The BIFR has sanctioned
revival plans in case of 12 PSEs  which are under implementation.  Government, on its own, has approved restructuring
in 6 other cases.  Attempts are being made for converting some of the companies into joint venture companies.  Since the
formation of the Department of Disinvestment, cases of 15 PSEs have been sent to that Department for Joint Venture
formation/disinvestment.  It has been decided to close/wind up 8 unviable PSEs and the prescribed procedures in this
regard are in progress, the Department added.
 
2.5          Even after the persistent efforts of the Ministry, the performance of the PSEs has been below the projected
levels. The Committee feels that the PSEs are required to put in more efforts to usher in a prosperous future.
              
 
III.       RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT OF AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY
 
3.1       The Department stated that R&D and technology development is the backbone of the automotive industry.
Because of this fact, a cess has been imposed on Automobiles with effect from 1.1.1984 and on tractors from 1.10.1985
at the rate of 18% ad-valorem to finance R&D in the industry. The cess is being collected by the Department of Revenue
and forms part of the Consolidated Fund of India. The Ministry of Finance is allocating a Portion of this fund through the
Budget to this Ministry under the head “Cess for the Development Council for Automobile and Allied Industries”.
 
3.2       It was also stated that with the fragmented automobile industry in India, it is not feasible for the individual units
to establish full-fledged R&D set up and testing facilitates. Hence there is a need to establish  R&D testing  facilities
which will cater  to the industry as a whole. With the  introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety
standards , more & more  R&D facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of the Industry, it was added. The
Department further added that the Development Council for Automotive and Allied Industry (DCAAI) allocates  Cess
funds for research and development to establish R&D institutions through a Cess Committee chaired by Secretary,
Department of  Heavy Industry. 
 
3.3       The Secretary during the course of his oral evidence informed the Committee that  there is tremendous need for
creating the testing facilities in the country as well as having R&D projects. He also informed the Committee that the
DHI have constituted the Development Council of Automotive Sector and  have established a Committee  to  authorize
and recommend use of R&D and testing facilities. The Secretary also mentioned to the Committee that  0.05% cess

may  not  be sufficient looking at the requirement of fund that has emerged.
              
3.4          It was further stated by the Secretary that in view of Euro II and Euro III norms,  considerable investment in
testing facilities will have to be generated, and also, DHI  have to provide for testing to see that the imported new and
old cars  conform to CMVR norms. Therefore, there is an added requirement for testing facilities, he felt. He also stated
that  there is a need now to set up at least two testing tracks, one in  the North and another in the South. In view of all
this, the cess needs to be raised to 0.25%, the Secretary felt.  It was revealed by the Secretary,  that the Department had
got Rs.10 crores for utilization from the Cess Fund which  is also insufficient. This will have to be considerably
increased if the DHI wants  to give fillip to R&D and testing facilities, he felt.
 
3.5       The Secretary also informed the Committee that there is need for promoting electric vehicles. He also felt that
there is need for having nominal custom and excise duties for electric vehicles and also for subsidy through the
Department of Non-Conventional Sources of Energy for three wheelers that they were giving for larger vehicles. 
 
3.6       The Committee  feels that the  cess  which  has been used till now for creating facilities for conducting test as per
Central Motor Vehicle Rules needs to be  used for  other areas  of product and process related research with a view to
giving a fillip to   India’s  automobile industries.  It is also necessary to enable the  automobile industries to survive   the 
imports  surge after WTO regime became fully applicable.  The  Committee  recommends that the Ministry should  take
stock of what is being done and what  further is to be done.  R&D  has  to be undertaken for product and process related
research also.
 
3.7       The Committee understands that the cess of 0.05%, which is being charged at  present, needs to be increased to
0.25% for  making   necessary investment in testing  facilities.  The Committee agrees with the view expressed by the
Secretary that the allocation of Rs. 10 crores, that  has been made, is insufficient  as R&D  and testing facilities  have to
be enhanced.  Therefore, Ministry of Finance may consider increasing at RE stage.
 
3.8       The Committee also  agrees  with the views expressed by the Secretary that the need of the hour is electric
vehicles for having pollution free transportation  in the cities, particularly, in the metropolises. The Government   may
consider exemption of customs duty and surcharge on items imported for use in manufacture of electric vehicles and
reduction of excise duty on electric vehicles. The Ministry of Non-Conventional  Sources of  Energy  may  also consider 
providing  subsidies to the extent of 50% to three  wheelers and the Department of Heavy Industry may  pursue the
matter in this regard.
 
3.9       The Department  have also  informed  the Committee that after  India  became  compliant with the WTO regime
with effect from 01-04-2001, quantitative restrictions on imports, regulations regarding local content in manufacture and
export obligations would  not be admissible. Import of automotive vehicles of all categories would  become permissible..
In order to address the following issues, the Ministry is in the process of formulating a comprehensive  holistic policy
compatible with the WTO regime:-
(i)
                  Exalt the sector as a lever of industrial growth and employment.
(ii)                Promote a globally competitive automotive industry and emerge as a global source for auto
components.
(iii)               Enable the development of a domestic safety and environmental regulatory structure for the
sector.
(iv)              Facilitate indigenous design, research and development.
 
3.10     The Committee  feels that the policy compatible with  WTO regime should have been formulated  much   before 
the regime became fully operational.  At least now, there should not be any further delay in formulating the Policy.

plan equity .   In addition, an amount of Rs.0.68 crores was utilized for payment of salary/wages to the employees of
National Instruments Ltd.

5.2          It was also stated that against the Department of Heavy Industry’s Demand  of  Rs.250.00 crores for the  revival

achieved.

Statutory Dues which was increased to Rs. 380.00 crores in RE stage. Explaining the reasons, the Department have

VIII. PLAN INVESTMENT IN PUBLIC SECTOR
 
8.1       The Plan allocation was raised from Rs. 138.00 crore (BE  2000-2001) to Rs. 354.82 crore (RE 2001-2002) in
order to release Plan equity of Rs. 250.00 crore to HMT Ltd, as per their revival Plan. For the year 2001-2002, an
amount of Rs. 231.55 crore was projected under Plan for the investment programmes of PSEs (Rs. 123.18 cr.) and
towards VRS expenditure (Rs. 108.37 cr.). Planning Commission has allocated Rs. 178.00 cr. only comprising a

provision of Rs. 70.00 crore for VRS expenditure and of Rs. 108.00 cr. for the investment programmes of PSEs.
 
8.2       The Department have also stated  that the plan allocation in 2001-2002 envisages a total outlay of Rs.549.17
crore with a Budgetary support of Rs.178.00 crores, which includes a  provision of Rs.16.94 crore  for meeting the
demands of PSEs for crucial balancing investments for improving their productivity  and viability.
8.3       The Annual Plan outlay of Rs.549.17 crore for 2001-2002 is planned to be funded by way of internal and extra
budgetary resources (IEBR) of Rs.371.17 crore and the balance of Rs.178.00 crore  through budgetary support from the 
Government.  Actual generation of internal resources  shall depend on the operational  performance of these PSEs 
during the year  which in  turn will depend  upon the order booking, etc.  Plan/non-plan support requirements  of PSEs 
during 2001-2002 shall be received at revised estimates stage.
 
8.4       The plan investment  provides  for budgetary support  for PSEs   by way of loans and equity mostly in the ratio
of  50:50  for taking up continuing schemes/projects for development, diversification, debottlenecking , modernization,
renewal, replacement, etc. to improve their  overall performance and viability.
 
8.5       The Committee noted that the Plan allocation was raised from Rs.138 crores in BE 2000-2001 to  Rs.354.8 crores
in RE but for the year 2001-2002 out of total projected requirement of Rs.231.55 crores only, Rs.178 crores has been
allocated.
 
8.6       In view of the present revival  schemes in various public sector undertakings and implementation of VRS, the
amount allocated is not sufficient and may be considered for increase as per the requirement at RE stage. The Committee
also hopes that the PSEs would be able to raise IEBR to the tune of Rs.371.17 crores as projected for 2001-2002.
 
8.7       The Committee recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should make conscious efforts to utilize the  
plan allocation made for modernization, renewal/replacement, implementation of  sanctioned  revival scheme, etc.  so
that  the PSEs could regain their vigour.
 
 
IX. NON-PLAN LOANS TO PSEs
9.1       Non-plan funds  are provided as loans to loss making PSEs, mostly to meet their cash losses; partly or in full,
depending on the availability  of funds.  In 2001-2002 an amount of   Rs.385.60 crores has been provided, which
includes Rs.150.00 crore for the implementation of restructuring schemes of some of the PSEs, Rs.150.00 crores for
payment   of employees   related statutory dues in unviable sick PSEs and  Rs.64.60 crores  for payment of dues other  
than ex-gratia to the employees of PSEs, who will be retired under VRS.
 
9.2       Explaining the reasons about the allocation of  non-plan loans to many PSEs, the Department has stated that  the
permission for closure of RIC, WIL and MNPM has already been received from the Ministry of Labour. Cases of closure
of NBCIL, BPMEL, MAMC, TAFCO, TCIL(Tangra) are under the consideration of Ministry of Labour/Ministry of
Law. The BIFR sanctioned scheme in respect of NIL is under implementation and it does not envisage any non plan
Budgetary support during 2001-2002. BOGL is under reference to BIFR and its revival plan is yet to be finalised. In
view of this, no non-plan allocation has been sought during the year 2001-2002 for these PSEs, the Department stated.
 
9.3       It was also stated that the additional requirement of  non-plan loans during 2000-2001 was on account of the
implementation of VSS (Rs.229.50 crores), payment of outstanding statutory dues (Rs.150.00 crores.), payment of dues
other than ex-gratia to the employees opting for VRS (Rs.52.00 crores.) This has necessitated an increase in the
allocation of non-plan funds in RE 2000-2001.
              
9.4          The Committee feels that, in case, decision for closure is taken in respect of some of the above mentioned
companies, the amount allocated under VSS  and Statutory Dues may  not be sufficient. Government may, therefore,

XIV.  GENERAL PROBLEMS OF PAPER INDUSTRY
 
14.1     Newsprint industry has been traditionally at a disadvantageous position due to lower return on its capital
employed, causing investments to go to higher returnable sectors. The opportunity costs entailed due to the above
scenario could have been obviated by appropriate policy instrument. However, abolition of QRs as a result of WTO
commitment has hit the newsprint harder and the 1:2 procurement condition now will have to be disbanded. Also, other
non-tariff barriers also have caused to be removed leading to inclusion of newsprint under the Open General License. In
this scenario the only ray of light to enable this industry to survive or turn-around is through the systematic tariff regime.
However, it is observed that a progressive and systematic tariff regime has been denied to this industry.  While the bound
rate under the WTO is 35%, the customs duty at present is at 5%. Besides, many of the intermediaries used in the 
manufacture of newsprint also attract very high custom duty rates. This type of customs tariff structure is not
commensurate with the fiscal logic, which accords higher custom duty on end products than the intermediaries. 
 
14.2     Hence, the Committee recommends that the Government may not only consider raising the custom’s duty to the
WTO bound level but also a TARIFF REALIGNMENT exercise may be taken up by the government to enable this
industry  to be accorded a level playing field for realizing higher productivity.
 
14.3     The Committee also observed that the industry has been recently putting a lot of efforts towards replenishment of
critical forests, which are used in newsprint products. This replenishment effort of the industry should be strongly
supported by the government not only to ensure present ecological balance but also as a futuristic measure. The
Committee hence strongly recommends that a proactive support be extended to the industry  in terms of relaxing or
expediting the necessary administrative clearance for this noble exercise of the industry.
 
14.4     During the course of examination of Demands for Grants of Ministry of Heavy Industry,  the performance review
of HPC and NEPA  mills, the Committee observed certain anomalies in the excise/customs tariff classification of papers
and paperboards. The paper and paperboards are classified under the same heading. It is felt that while the end products
are distinctly different, even the manufacturing process involved is also different. The paperboard is made out of waste
recycling through non-conventional source and needs to be classified differently from paper, which, inter-alia, should
cover newsprint papers, etc. In this context it also came to the light that there is an excise duty exemption availed by
paper and newspaper manufacturers as well as paper board manufacturers producing upto 3500 MT annually. During the
investigation,  it came to the light of the committee that the mills are operating at sub-optimal capacity restricting their
production to 3500 MTs, enabling them to avail of this excise duty exemption.
 
14.5     The Committee  recommends that this anomaly needs to be corrected through distinguishing paper from
paperboard by virtue of differently classifying or sub-classifying one product from another. As regards duty exemption,
it is felt that the same should be based on installed capacity of the units and not annual production as such a provision is
vulnerable to abuse resulting in sub-optimal utilization of the capacity by units, which can also, amongst other things,
cause potential shortages of the products resulting in upward trend in prices of boards. 
 
14.6     The CMD, HNL informed the Committee that the quality of the imported newsprint from Canada is definitely
superior to our newsprint in terms of brightness. The price difference is about  Rs. 3000 per tonne. The advantage that
the countries like Canada, Europe, etc., have got is that they are having superior raw materials like spruce, pine, etc.,
where they can go in for lower g.s.m. newsprint. Now, every newspaper  publisher  wants to pay by weight and print by
metre. Newspaper publishing houses want to install machines which can print 1 lakh copies per hour, 40 pages at a time.
They are all going for high speed printing machines. With the kind of raw materials we are having in our country, we
will not be able to catch up to  that level, he added. To that extent, a lot of R&D is required to be done and the R&D
efforts are being done through the Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute,  in a modest way by the newspaper
manufacturers.
 
14.7     The Committee feels that the R&D efforts being made to improve the quality of newsprint are not to the extent it
is necessary. Looking at the present scenario, it  is very essential to catch-up with the best technology. Therefore, the

FKM of Optical Fibre Cables during the year 1999-2000.  The Turnkey Project Division achieved a turnover of Rs. 218
crores.  Overall the Company achieved turnover of Rs. 803.51 crores during 1999-2000 registering 350% growth over
the actual of Rs. 222.31 crores during 1998-99.
 
21.5        The Department also stated that after providing for interest and depreciation, the net loss came down to Rs.
39.32 crores from a level of Rs. 138.73 crores during the previous year 1998-99, also the net loss for the year 1999-2000
could be contained at a level of Rs. 39.32 crores as against Rs. 50.51 crores projected at the end of the first year of
implementation of the package.  In the current year 2000-01 the company has achieved a turnover of Rs. 592.18 crores
as against Rs.501.43 crores in the corresponding period previous year thereby registering a growth of 18%.  The
estimated net loss from April, 2000 to December, 2000 is Rs. 49.97 crores.   HCL has been provided a budget support of
Rs.13.50 crores in BE-2001-2002.

to enable the company to show upward graph. The Committee notes that DoT has reserved 25% of its requirement for
HCL.The Committee, however, realises that the limited orders placed to H.C.L. by other sister concerns in Govt. sector
is not enough to make the company viable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government  should help the
company in exploring market in the private sector as well as foreign countries with help of TCIL.
 
21.7     The Committee came to know that the company is having problem for taking loan from banks on higher rate of
interest which is eating into its profit which they have earned after putting valiant effort. The Committee recommends
that Govt. should stretch its helping hand to the company to sort out the problem in every possible manner.

associates itself with other Ministries and Organizations.
 
1.2
              The important   role  and  tasks of  the Department  of  Public  Enterprises  are:-
 
(i)        General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
(ii)       Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to    Public Sector Enterprises;
(iii)      Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial   management, personnel management, board structures, wage
settlement, training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
(iv)     All matters relating to Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the    Public    Sector Enterprises and
the Administrative Ministries / Departments.;
(v)       Matters relating to  the delegation of powers to Board of Directors;
(vi)     To undertake in-depth studies in respect of significant areas of functioning of central PSEs.;
(vii)Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE);
(viii)     Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE);
(ix)     To monitor and evaluate the performance of PSEs and to act as a repository of data and to bring out an
Annual Survey for the Parliament; and
(x)    Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators for settlement of   disputes among   Public Sector Enterprises and
Government Departments except disputes      relating to tax  matters.
1.3      The Department has five constituent Divisions, viz,  the Financial Policy Division, the Management Policy Division,
the MOU Division, the Administration & Coordination  Division and Permanent Machinery of Arbitration. The Financial
Policy Division comprises the Public Enterprises Survey Unit, the Policy Planning Unit, and the Wage Policy Unit. The
Management Policy Division comprises the personnel policy unit, training unit, performance indicator and work norms unit
(PIWN Unit) and SC & ST Cell. The MOU Division comprises MOU Unit, Data Bank and Computer Cell. The
Administration & Coordination Division comprises the Administration, Library, Parliament and Coordination Wings and
Hindi Cell. The Permanent Machinery of Arbitration (PMA) provides a forum for settlement of commercial disputes
between two or more PSEs as well as between a Government Department and PSEs.

III.       SEARCH COMMITTEE AND NAVRATNAS &   MINIRATNAS
 
3.1       The Ministry stated that a  Search Committee is set up with the approval of the Cabinet for selecting   non-official part
time Directors for Navratna and Miniratna PSUs.The Search Committee selects non-official part time Directors of impeccable
stature and background for induction of at least 4 non-official Directors in the case of Navratna PSEs and 3 non-official
Directors in the case of Miniratna PSEs.  Non-official part time Directors are drawn from Public men, Technocrats,
Management Experts & Consultants and Professional Managers in Industry & Trade with high degree of proven ability.  They
play a complimentary role in providing professional and managerial advice to the Board and are appointed with the approval
of ACC on part time basis.
 
3.2       Professionalisation of the Boards of Public Enterprises  is one of the thrust areas of Public Sector Reforms as it is vital

VI.    MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
6.1       Under  the present set-up of the Department of Public Enterprises, the MoU Division is one of the five constituent
Divisions of the Department of Public Enterprises which co-ordinates the entire exercise of finalizing the Memorandum of 
Understandings  (MoUs) in respect of all the Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) numbering about 108.  The New
Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis of the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the
MoU system.
6.2       With the advent of the privatization and globalisation in Indian Economy mainly after the implementation of  New
Industrial Policy of 1991, the Central PSEs have been exposed to the domestic and international competition. Now, these 
PSEs  have   to   compete  with  the    Private  Sector  in   the   consumer  economy. In such a stiff competitive environment, it
is essential for a PSE to have an edge of both cost and quality over its competitors. MoU system has been accepted by the
PSEs as a panacea  since it has given them more freedom to take decisions independently  and operate more effectively and
proficiently.
 
6.3     The Government of India following the recommendation of the Arjun Sengupta Committee introduced the MOU
system. The MOU system has grown at a steady rate and from 4 MOUs signed in the year 1987-88  it has grown to  108 PSEs
which have  signed MoUs for the year 1999-2000.
 
6.4       The main objective of the MOU system was to improve the performance of the PSEs through the mechanism of
increased autonomy and accountability and also to provide a uniform method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner. Further, it was also envisaged to provide a clarity of
goals/objectives to be achieved by PSEs.
6.5       The purpose of the MOU system are to :
 
(i)
      Measure the performance of PSEs taking into account the complexity of fusing social and financial objectives
and translating them into measurable parameters:
(ii)    Ensure simultaneous increase in autonomy as well as accountability;
(iii)   Set up new institutions and administrative & personnel systems;
(iv)  Replace `multiple principles with multiple objectives’ with clarity in goals and objectives;
(v)    Break the vicious circle of NOT ME syndrome.
 
6.6       The Department of Public Enterprises provides a neutral forum for finalising the MOUs which is essential to make it
an objective system. The Department provides the entire technical and analytical inputs such as preparation of the common
guidelines for drafting of MOUs, preparation of background notes and critiques on the draft MOUs submitted by the PSEs,
Organisation of MOU negotiation and evaluation meetings, etc., of the expert group called Ad-Hoc Task Force(ATF) in order
to finalise the MOUs and evaluate the performance of the PSEs at the end of the year. Department of Public Enterprises
ensures that the entire MOU exercise is carried out in an objective, transparent and broad based manner.
 
6.7       It acts as the permanent  secretariat to the HPC and ATF. The main functions of the MoU Division are:
·
        To provide logistical support to the Ad-Hoc Task Force.  It is expected to provide not only administrative
support but also technical support to the Ad-Hoc Task Force.
·        To act as buffer between the Ad-Hoc  Task  Force  members and the   signatories to  the MoUs, i e,  PSEs   and
Administrative  Ministries .  It is  expected  that ATF   members will have contacts with signatories to MoU 
through  MoU Division only.
·        To  develop information and data base on various PSEs signing MoU.
·        To  prepare agenda and background papers for the  High Power Committee.
·        To monitor the progress of  the MoUs.  The MoU  Division keeps a watch  on various stages involving in the
preparation of MoUs to ensure that all parties involved in the process adhere to the relevant  guidelines and
deadlines.
·        To  provide advice  and counsel to the MoU signatories on methodological and conceptual aspects  of the
MoU  Policy.
·        To coordinate research  and training on various aspects  of MoU Policy.
 
6.8       During the oral evidence , Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that  expenditure 
reforms  commission have recommended that the work relating to the preparation and evaluation of MoU could be left  to the

48th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/48threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:26]
Administrative Ministries and  MoU Division would be abolished.
 
6.9       On a query as to  whether the object of signing MoUs would be achieved in the absence of a over-seeing agency, i.e.
Department of Public Enterprises, the  Department felt that an overseeing  body like DPE is essential for implementation of
the MoU system to fully achieve the objectives of MoU system .
 
6.10     If the task of preparation and evaluation of MoU is given to the same Administrative Ministry then the main feature of
MoU system, i.e objectivity, neutrality and transparency would suffer. Also there will be no uniform method to cross compare
the performance of the PSEs in other Ministries as being done at present by the Department of Public Enterprises, the
Department felt. Moreover,  objectivity, neutrality and transparency would suffer.
 
6.11        It was agreed that a Ministry can not act as a third neutral party in the process of negotiating and finalising the MoUs
between the Ministry and the PSE under that Ministry.   This will lead to  setting up of  mutual  admiration  club. Under the
present system, all policy issues relating to the MoU system are dealt with by the HPC through DPE in a  centralised manner.
If administrative Ministries are to implement the MoU system, in that case each Ministry will have to approach the HPC
separately.  This will  usher in  an era  of cacophony leaving behind  the era of cohesion.
 
6.12        It was further stated that in case MoU is to be prepared, evaluated and monitored by same Ministry, then separate
unit with some experts will have to be given the task. Such a step  would invite requirement of a large staff strength taking all
the Ministries together as compared to one small single unit of MoU Division in the Department of Public Enterprises.
 
6.13        If preparation/evaluation etc. of MoU is in the same Administrative Ministry, then the influence on concerned public
sector undertakings under that Ministry would obviously make MoU infructuous.
 
6.14       After hearing the  Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises, the Committee expressed its   unhappiness  that the
Expenditure Reforms Commission has recommended that the task of preparing MoUs can be left as well to the concerned
administrative Ministries.  The Committee feels that  the said Commission  in an anxiety  to reduce the  Government
expenditure under mined the role  of   a  nodel agency, i.e. , Department of Public Enterprises without  evaluating  its
performance over the years .
 
6.15        The Committee is also of the view that a unified central agency to implement the MoU system is certainly more cost
effective rather than having separate MoU Units in all the Administrative Ministries. Similarly, pooling expertise  for all the
Ministries from the same ATF as is being done at present by the Department of Public Enterprises is also cost effective.
 
6.16        The Committee  further   feels  that  the  Department  of  Public  Enterprises   provides  a neutral  forum  for 
finalising  the  MoUs, which  is   essential   to make it an objective system, and it should not be abolished.
 
6.17       The Committee is also  of the firm view that  the object of signing MoUs would not be achieved in the absence of an
over-seeing agency, i.e., the Department of Public Enterprises.
 
6.18        The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the proposal of abolishing MoU Division may be shelved. As
the country is now on the threshold of making PSEs  more vibrant, productive and efficient, it is very essential that the MoU
Division should be further strengthened instead of being abolished. Strengthening of MoU Division would go a long way in
making PSEs profitable and responsive to competitiveness.
 
6.19        The Committee, therefore, again recommends that   the Department of Public Enterprises should be strengthened so
as to make it more responsive.

REPORT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) is the nodal ministry for policy
formulation, promotion, development and protection of small scale industries. It also monitors the implementation of
these policies.
 
1.2       Ministry of SSI & ARI designs  and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and
growth of small and tiny enterprises, including the coir industries. The Ministry also coordinates with other
Ministries/Departments on behalf the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector.
 
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO), statutory bodies/other organizations like Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) and Coir Board; a
Public Sector Undertaking – National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC); and three training institutes – National
Institute of Small Industry Extension Training  (NISIET), Hyderabad; National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small
Business Development (NIESBUD), New Delhi and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati.
 
1.4       The Committee has been given to understand that small industry continues to get the benefits as long as it
remains small. As soon as it attains the status of a medium scale, it becomes ineligible for such benefits. The 
Department,  in this  connection, have informed the Committee that the Abid Hussain Committee examined the
jurisdiction of the Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro and Rural Industries and observed as under:
 
“ The Department of Small Scale  Industries  is  conceived to  be  structured as an umbrella body for the promotion of
small enterprises.  Since, this department is  now envisaged to promote small scale enterprises in general, the Expert 
Group  recommends that  its nomenclature be  now changed to the Department of Small scale Industries and Business
Enterprises.”
 
1.5       The Committee has also been informed that the  Expenditure  Reforms  Commission examined the issue   of re-
defining the role of the  Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries.  The Commission examining
the issue at  length  felt that it is the opportune time to review the policy  for the growth of small  sector to include not
merely small scale industries but also small establishments in the fast expanding service sector.  The committee also 
made the  following observations:
 
“To the extent that governmental support  on a graded scale is    required to be provided to small and medium 
establishments it would be appropriate  to rename  the Ministry of Small Industries and Agro and Rural Industries as
Ministry of Small and  Medium  Establishments.”
 
1.6       The Committee observes  that the idea of having  small and  medium  Enterprises instead  of having 
compartmentalized   small scale industries has become a global concept .  If Government  support is  given to small and
medium enterprises,  it will have  salutary  effect   on the economy.
 
1.7         The Committee, however, would like to discuss the issue with all concerned before coming to a conclusion and
making any recommendation in this regard.
 
1.8       With the removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) as part of WTO commitments, the SSIs are faced with new
challenges. Reduction of tariffs and dismantling of non-tariff  barriers has resulted in opening up of imports and
increased competition in all product categories, including those  items, which have been exclusively reserved for
manufacture in the small-scale sector. As the imports surge, relatively cheaper and qualitatively superior foreign goods
will be flooding the market. As a consequence the most affected sector will be  the SSI sector.
 
1.9       Ministry’s role at this juncture becomes of paramount importance as it has to evolve
mechanisms/directives/guidelines which will go a long way in shaping the course of  things in future.   In view of these

49th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/49threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:26]
threats,  safeguarding the interests of indigenous  industry is the major responsibility of  the Ministry while formulating
policies.  Government should provide  level playing field  for  the small scale industry to meet the  challenges of stiff 
competition from  global  players.
 
1.10     The Committee has been given to understand that the competitive fervor unleashed by the liberalization process
has led to a paradigm shift in the nature of manufacturing activity in the country. In such a scenario it has become
imperative that the policy of protection for  small scale sector  should pave its  way to a more proactive approach of
helping such units to enhance their competitiveness in a market driven economy. If small and  tiny enterprises have to
compete in globalized environment they now require an enabling and responsive environment  which provides adequate
and timely credit and pragmatic institutional, technological and infrastructural support. The Committee hopes that the
above proposals announced in the budget would mitigate the hardships faced by the SSI sector. The Government should,
however, not feel complacent about this.The Committee has noted that the budget for 2001-02 has made the following
proposals which are aimed at providing an impetus for growth of the SSI sector:
 
      -     Excise duty exemption on SSI raised from Rs.50 lakh to Rs. I crore for the small scale sector.
Provisions of budgetary support of Rs. 100 crore for the new  Credit Guarantee Scheme (CGS) in the current year. The
limit of loan without collateral raised from Rs. IO lakh to Rs.25 lakh under this scheme.
The items related to leather goods,  shoes and toys dereserved.
Accelerated depreciation  at  the rate of 50 percent on plant and machinery  purchased under the Technology
Upgradation Fund  Scheme for weaving, processing and garment sectors of the textile industry.
 
1.11.    During the course of oral evidence one of the representatives of Industrial  associations  stated :   “Sir, one of the
biggest  problems we faced in the SSI sector is that of rules and regulations, different Acts, etc. If they are simplified,
then it will make a big  difference.   Sir, Inspector Raj is   one of the biggest  problems of the SSI sector.  It has come
out of the laws which have with us.  We  have the Government Interaction  Cost (GIC).  That also is extremely high, at
the moment.  The  amount of money which we has to be passed on to the inspectors  is very  substantial.   Therefore, 
we want reduction  in that cost.  It  should  come down” Another   representative informed  committee:  there are so
many inspectors  who  come to the small entrepreneurs. If these problems  are taken  care of, then the Indian 
entrepreneurs are  capable of facing the world  competition.    If  he is not harassed on those issues, then he would 
concentrate his time on marketing his products, etc.”
 
1.12     In  view  of the above the  Committee feels that adequate steps are  required to  be taken to  remove   the
Inspector  Raj.  The Committee also recommends that simplification  of  rules, regulation and  amendment of labour   
laws   may be  done  so that   SSI  units are  not subject to unnecessary harassment.    The Ministry  of SSI  and Agro &
Rural Industries may  take up the  matter with the concerned  administrative ministries.  By taking these measures, the
Committee feels that SSI sector would get a level  playing field to   a large extent.

X         CREDIT
 
10.1     The Committee has been informed that  lack of adequate and  timely credit is a frequent complaint of the  small
scale industry. Besides, there is no dedicated credit delivery system for SSI. Representatives of industrial associations
added that banks insist on collateral, which the small entrepreneurs, with limited resources, are unable to furnish. The
Committee has also noted with dismay that tiny and low budget investment is discouraged by the banks. The Ministry
has apprised the Committee in this regard  that the major thrust during the current year is to implement the policy
package announced by the Prime Minister in August, 2000. The important aspects of this policy comprise of Credit 
Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology  Upgradation  and a Credit Guarantee Scheme to provide collateral free
loan to SSI  units.  In the package a provision of Rs.100 crore for  new Credit Guarantee Scheme to encourage banks to
lend to the small and tiny sector,  without insisting on collateral has been made SIDBI will also contribute Rs.25 crores
making it a total of Rs.125 crores in the ratio of 4:1. It was envisaged to enhance the corpus fund size to Rs 2500 crores
in five years time. The Committee has, however, been informed by some representatives of industry that even when the
policy package has been announced, the banks are still reluctant to give loans. A period of about eight months have
since elapsed and the proposal is yet to  take off, it was added.
 
10.2     The Committee recommends that   the policy package for credit guarantee scheme may be made  operational at
the earliest in case it has not been made as yet.   The Committee also feels that the lengthy bureaucratic red tapism in
clearing credit needs to be removed and rules  be simplified and made easy.
 
The Committee  is also of the view that the amount allocated under the scheme is too meager to serve a meaningful
purpose considering the gross under-financing of the sector by the banks. Hence the Committee recommends that the
provision under the scheme may  be  enhanced substantially in initial years. The larger the size of the corpus in the
initial years , the better credibility and viability of the scheme.

12.1     When the Secretary was asked to comment on Bill Discounting System and  possibility of its introduction in SSI

manufacturer has also to accept those  Bills because the small scale entrepreneurs are not so strong and the large

XIII      SMALL INDUSTRIES DEVELOPMENT BANK OF INDIA (SIDBI)
 
13.1     SIDBI is the principal financial institution for small scale industries which financies units having  investment in
plant and machinery upto Rs.100 lakh. While the world over , the concept of small and medium enterprises is more
prevalent, this statutory restriction  prevents SIDBI  from  operating widely which affects  the  competitiveness of
SIDBI vis-à-vis commercial bank and othe Development Financing Institutions (DFIs).
 
13.2     The Committee therefore recommends that SIDBI should enlarge the scope of  its assistance to small and
medium enterprises. Expansion by SIDBI  in the operational canvas will generate additional revenue for SIDBI thus
helping it to undertake more promotional and developmental activities for strengthening tiny/SSI Sector in the WTO
regime.
 
13.3     Due to continued sizable assistance at below the cost of funds under refinance, special schemes of assistance and
various promotional and developmental activities, there has been squeeze on the spirit available to SIDBI particularly in
the last few years. SIDBI has been requesting Government of India to allow access to concessional sources of funding to
enable the Bank to continue concessional lending to SSIs and take developmental activities in tandem with the policy
prescriptions of Government of India in the WTO regime.
 
13.4     The Committee recommends that Ministry should impress upon the Ministry of Finance/RBI to assist SIDBI  for
raising low cost resources so as to remain viable while taking up various developmental activities in the SSI sector.
 
13.5     The Union Budget 2001-02 has, interalia, withdrawn the tax-exempt status hitherto available to SIDBI under
Section 50 of SIDBI Act. This would have a negative impact on the profitability and viability of SIDBI particularly
when no other perceptible form of resource support is made available to the Bank. This may also have an adverse
impact on the rating of SIDBI  which is already under strain on account of proposed transfer of SFCs shareholding from
IDBI to SIDBI.
 
13.6     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tax - exempt status as provided in the Small Industries
Development Bank of India (Amendment) Act,  2000,  may be retained. Ministry of Finance may be approached to
restore the status of SIDBI as before.
 
13.7     While it is desirable that SIDBI should operate on a larger canvass, it would also be appropriate to rope in
private banks for financing purposes. In that case government would have to extend tax benefits to these  financial
institutions when they lend to tiny units.

XV       SUPPORT TO FIGHT ANTI DUMPING PRACTICES
 
15.1     The small scale sector finds itself constrained from meeting the threat posed by dumping on account of their
unorganized nature, ignorance, lack of necessary data and limited resource availability, the representatives of industrial
organisations informed.
 
15.2     Hence the Committee suggests  that financial and legal assistance be provided by the government to fight the
anti - dumping cases abroad and for filing antidumping petitions within the country.
 
15.3     The Committee observes that it takes 90 days to review economic fallout of imported goods in country and 
imposition of  anti-dumping duty thereon. By that time huge financial losses would  have already occurred   to the
country which are irretrievable. The Committee observes that in order to preclude the possibility of economic losses,
anti-dumping monitoring should be expedited. The Committee therefore recommends that the administrative ministry
should review the pros and cons in this regard and take timely action. The system that exists in other countries may be
examined. India can also emulate such a system.
 
15.4     The Committee was informed by the Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries  and Agro and Rural
Industries that in America there exists a law under which on a complaint, antidumping duty is imposed on the imported
goods in the first instance.  After considering all pros and cons only, a decision will be taken either to lift ban or
continue it.
 
15.5     The Committee understands that enacting law in this matter is not the concern of this ministry.  The Committee,
therefore,  recommends that the matter may be taken up with the concerned administrative ministry for making a law, if
necessary.  Otherwise necessary regulations may be prepared by the concerned Ministry and the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries   and Agro & Rural Industries  may pursue it.
 
15.6     One of the representatives of the industries stated that even if we were not able to hold the imported goods with
tariff barriers, but at least we can have non-tariff barriers.  We can ask them to comply with our regulations.  Printing of
MRP should be made compulsory on the imported goods.  Similarly, these goods should comply with ISI regulations. 
He was confident that by these steps, we can stop dumping of goods.
 
15.7     Secretary informed the Committee that the provisions related to MRP  as well as ISI mark should apply in the
same manner on the imported goods as they apply to the indigeniously manufactured items.  Any packed commodity
that is  sold in India shall have to have the year of manufacturing, expiry date and  maximum retail price.  Any importer
can sell his imported goods in India only when he meets these requirements.  The items should also indicate  the
contents  inside the pack.  Wherever it is written in the concerned country’s  language then it shall have the English
version also.  Similarly, he informed the Committee that  the imported items should meet the Indian standard just as in
the case of indigenously  manufactured products.   He  further stated that they had implemented these things four

this regard and implemented expeditiously.
 
XVI     RATIONALIZATION OF TAXES AND TARIFFS FOR SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
 
16.1     There is an urgent need for rationalization and simplification of tax structure to enhance the competitiveness of
small scale industry. While the budget has   endeavored to rationalize the tax structure, some anomalies still remain.
Some of  the problems faced by SSIs with respect to distortions arising out of iniquitous tax structure, have been 
brought to the notice of the Committee.
 
16.2     For the cable industry, while cables are allowed to be imported at the basic customs duty of 15 percent or 25
percent, the raw material which goes into the manufacture of cables has a basic customs duty of 35 percent plus 16
percent CVD plus 4 percent Special Auxillary Duty (SAD). This increases the cost of production of the domestic
manufacturer as compared to the     imported product. There is an urgent need to take remedial measures to rationalize
the  customs duty on raw materials.       
 
16.3     The Committee  suggests that the SAD on raw material be made MODATABLE as this would reduce the raw
material cost.
 
16.4     The Committee was also informed that  granite and marble  industries  should be  treated at par . It was also
stated that  in the edible  oil Industry, the running mills  have to pay  75%  duty were as  the sick  units have to pay 55%
duty and   this differential duty  for sick. Mill and running mill should not be there.  It   was also pointed out during the
course of discussion  that the  limit of  one crore rupees on roller  bearings industry has been removed.  It was felt that 
there should be one crore rupees limit.   The Committee appreciates  that most of these  demands have been met  by the
Government  in the recent budget.
 
16.5     The Committee recognizes that special and friendly relations exist between India and Nepal in all spheres of
activities including bilateral trade. The manufacturers’ representatives of vanaspati, silk, woolen, copper wire, etc.
operating in the small scale sector explained their difficulties vis-à-vis the imports from Nepal. These representatives
mentioned that the manufacturers in Nepal have an edge over them in pricing of their products in as much as they are
allowed import of raw-material at zero customs duty. The Indian  manufacturers, however, have to pay customs duty on
imported raw-material.
 
16.6     The Committee would like the Ministry to look into this aspect of unfair competition being posed by the imports
from Nepal. The Committee understands that the Indo-Nepal Trade Treaty is due for review during the later part of
2001. It would, therefore, recommend that this matter may be looked into and corrective measures taken.
 
16.7     The  Committee also desires that the items like footwear, agricultural implements etc. used by the poorer
sections of the society should be available at cheaper prices. Government may consider reducing taxes on such items.
 
XVII    MARKETING

17.1     Marketing companies are assuming an increasingly important role in the emerging competitive environment.
The Committee has been informed that  marketing outfits in all the developing economies have the prime role in
marketing of products. Our banking sector does not recognize marketing as an essential activity for SMEs and,
therefore, adequate financing is not available for the sector.
 
17.2     The Committee, therefore, is of the view  that the marketing and distribution companies need to be considered
for being  given the status of industry for the purpose of getting financial assistance from banks and Fls as well as lead
institutions.
 
17.3     Marketing and developing brand image of the SSI products also has not been handled effectively. The role of
KVIC in marketing the products has been increased in Budget 2000-2001, but no new marketing techniques or
involvement of private institutions have been envisaged.
 
17.4     The Committee  recommends promotion of private sector participation in marketing of SSI products through
proper incentives like granting  tax relief in a manner similar to 80 HHC currently available on exports for companies
marketing SSI products.
 
XVIII   EXPORTS BY SSI SECTOR
 
18.1     The SSI sector in India covers a wide spectrum of industries categorized under small, tiny and cottage segments
ranging from small artisan/handicraft units to modern production units with significant investments and produces a vide
range of products exceeding 7500. The industrial policy 1990 laid emphasis on the steps to enhance the contribution of
SSI sector in  overall exports,  employment  generation and   dispersal  of
industries in rural areas. 800 items are currently reserved for exclusive manufacture in the SSI sector although there is
no regulation or restriction on marketing the reserved items by large industries.
 
18.2     But the Committee notes with dissatisfaction  that even as the industrial policy laid emphasis on the steps to
enhance  the contribution of the SSI Sector in over all exports, the performance of the SSI sector in this regard  has been
disparaging  and the contribution is negligible.  The Committee feels that perhaps serious marketing efforts were not
made by those concerned and it was left to its own fate. Though Government has been extending preferences in respect
of purchase of items manufactured by SSIs and  a number of steps taken in the recent post reform period by the Govt.
like FDI, establishment of growth centers, export promotion, marketing etc. exports of SSI products have not taken off 
at the expected level.
 
18.3     The Committee, therefore, observes that efforts made for export of SSI products are inadequate and  there is
need to improve the quality of products for this purpose.
 
18.4     The Committee also  recommends that exports should be increased by making SSI products qualitatively better
and cost effective.
 
XIX     PROBLEM OF DELAYED PAYMENTS TO SSI UNITS
 
19.1     The Committee has been given to  understand that at present Balance Sheet of the Companies indicate the
amount due to SSI units. But interest due to SSI units on account of delayed payment is not shown separately. As a
result, there is no authentic source on which the Income Tax authorities can rely to disallow the interest due, payable or
paid by any buyer in accordance with the Delayed Payment Act, 1993 for the purposes of computation of income under
Income Tax Act 1961 as deduction.
 
19.2     The Committee, recommends that the interest due or payable or paid to SSI units on account of delayed
payments as per the provisions of the Delayed Payments Act 1993 (as amended) may be shown separately in the
Balance Sheet of Companies.

FIFTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. 
having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf , do hereb y present this Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the Status of the Sponge Iron Industri es und er the Ministry of Steel. 
2. The Committee in its sitting held on 28th June , 1993 considered a note receiv ed from the 
Ministry of Steel on Sponge Iron and decjded to send a questionnaire to the Ministr y on the 
subject for their replies. In its sitting held on 29th September , 1993, the Committe e heard the 
views of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel by way of clarifications to the repl ies sent by the 
Ministry to the said questionnaire. 
3. The Committee considered in depth the problems prevailing in sponge iron industr y and 
Government's efforts to protect its interests. The Committee had deliberations on the overall 
present scenario with a view to project the possible ways in salvaging the sponge Iron Indust ries. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its sitting held on the lOth February. 
1994. 
5. Based on the papers and other relevant material on the subject and also the evidence of 
the Secretary, the Committee had noted the following picture of the Sponge Iron indu stry in the 
country. 
5.1 Sponge iron is a partial substitute for steel melting Scrap. It is a met allic product 
produced by direct induction of high grade iron ore or pellets in the solid stat e i.e. without the 
material going into the liquid phase as in the blast furnace. It is also known as Direct Reduced 
Iron (DRI) or Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI). This reduction of iron ore can be achieved by using 
either carbon bearing material such as non-coking coal or a suitable redu cing gas produced by 
reforming of natural gas. On the other hand sponge iron can also be used in the integrated steel 
plants to replace steel melting scrap to some extent as a coolant in the LD convertors and as a 
part of the change mix in the basic oxygen furnace and open hearth furnace. 
5.2 Non-coking coal and natural gas are the two main ingredients in spong e iron technology. 
Earlier the technology was limited upto use. of non-coking coal but with the technological 
innovation gas based sponge iron plants have also been set up. While coal based technology 
involves reduction of iron ore in a rotary kiln using non-coking coal as a reduct ant, gas based one 
uses Hydrogen or Carbon Mono Oxide or a mixture of both as reductant s. Gas based sponge iron 
manufacturing process requires high-grade iron ore with around 65%. At present non-coking coal 
is imported for sponge iron industry. Less availability of high grade of iron ore and Jack of 
required allocation of natural gas have proved to be impediments in proper development of 
sponge iron industries. 
5.3 According to Government 's report , a number of steps have been taken to promote the 
sponge iron industry as a major thrust area. Broadly, the sponge iron industr y was delicensed in 
March, 1985. Then under the new industrial policy the requirement of obta ining registration for 
setting up new plants was dispensed with in 1991. Sponge iron is also includ ed in the list of "High 
Priority Industries" in the new policy. The production capacity of first coal based plant which was 
set up in 1981, has been doubled from 30,000 tpa to 60,000 tpa. Governm ent have also set up a 
Linkage Committee in the Ministry of Steel to assist the enterpreneures , inte rested in setting up 
sponge iron plants, by way of providing single window clearance for linkage in the production of 
coal and movement of coal and iron ore by the Railways. The Committee has been given to 
under stan d that the Ministry of Steel has been successful in pursuading the Ministry of Petroleum 

and Natural Gas with regard to allocation of natural gas for gas based sponge iron plants of a 
capacity of 4 million tonnes per annum. 
5.4 During the course of his evidence the Secretary, Ministry of Steel informed the Committee 
that at present Government have allocated natural gas to five sponge iron plants. These plants are 
namely (i) Essar Gujarat Ltd., Gujarat (ii) Grasim Industries Ltd., Maharashtra (iii) Nippon Demo 
!spat Ltd., Maharashtra (iv) Kalyani Steels Ltd ., Maharashtra and (v) Usha Rect ifire Ltd., U.P. He 
further informed that the Petroleum Ministry has got a priority list and gas is allocated mainly to 
the power and fertilizer sector. There is no surplus gas available for further allocat ion to any of 
steeVsponge iron plants. If an industrialist wants to set up a plant he approac hes the Ministry of 
Steel by way of filling up a memorandum opting for v~rious available linkages such as coal, gas, 
railways etc. and for such purpose a Linkage Committee has been set up in the Ministry to liaison 
on his behalf with the concerned authorities. 
5.5 The installed production capacity of sponge iron has increased. from 30,000 tones in 1980-81 
to about 18 lakh tonnes in 1992-93. The production during last 4 years has increased from 
1.9 lakh tonnes in 1988-89 to 12.8 lakh tonnes in 1991-92 as per the details given below:-

According to Government's estimate the annual production of company in 1992-93 was 
expected to be around 49,000 tonnes against the fixed target of 51,000 tonnes due to 
deterioration in the quality of coal supplied by Singareni Collieries, lower ash carbon contents in 
coal and adverse conditions of transportation of iron ore. 
5.6 The Committee has been informed by the Secretary that an installed capacity of 6 million 
tonnes of sponge iron would be created by the end of the Ylllth Five Year Plan. as against the 
Present installed capacity of 2.49 million tonnes. Various units are coming into operation from 
time to time while some other units are at different stages of completion. A majority of them will 
come into operat ion in the year 1994-95. Some units are likely to come into operation in the year 
1995-96. One unit will come into operation in 1996-97. All these projects were given linkages 
during Seventh Five Year Plan. The target so fixed is not a restrictive target and the same can go 
beyond that depending on dynamics and demand of the situation in the years to come. However 
he added that no investment is proposed to be made by Government in achieving the projected 
production targets and the entire additional capacity is expected to be set up in the private sector. 
Government would welcome the proposals from private enterpreneurs in that regard. According 
to the Secretary, Government have no information about expansion of capacity utilisation being 
undertaken, if any, by a specific private unit. The Committee has been given to understand that 
one lndustrial Enterpreneur's Memorandum has been filled for a sponge iron plant of 15,000 
tonnes per annum capacity in Goa. Government presumes that this would be coal based project 
but no request for coal linkage has been received by it from the ente rpreneur. Accordin g to the 
Secretary in such cases it is presumed that those who do not follow up their proposals , it mea ns 
they are not serious about their proposals. 
5. 7 The high cost of production has severely affected the capacity utilisati o n of sponge iron 
plants for which the present duty structure in mainl y responsible. Sponge Iron Manuf acturers 
Association and some sponge iron producers have repres ented against present dut y structur e with 
following requests:-
(i) reduction of customs duty on iron ore, iron ore pellets and non-coking coal in order to 
reduce the cost of raw material; 
(ii) keeping customs duty on imported scrap at a level that would allow sponge iro n 
producers to get a remunerative prices. 
According to Government's reports customs duty on iron ore has been brought down from 
90% to 20% and on iron ore pellets from 35% to 15% in the current year's budget. 
During the course of oral evidence the Secretary informed the Committee that their 
recommendations about providing non-coking coal facility to the producers is under consideration 

of the Finance Ministry. Another recommendation regarding reduction of import duty on scrap 
from 12% to 5% is also pending for considerat ion of the Ministry of Finance. According to the 
Secretary any proposal which goes from any Ministry to the Ministry of Finance for giving reliefs to 
the various industries is looked into by the Finance Ministry from the point of view of their effect 
on the overall revenue and resource position. Government are supporting the sponge iron industry 
to come up and its policies are attuned to see that sponge iron industry in India grows and at the 
same time to ensure that mini steel plants do not suffer. To maintain such balance a set of packages 
has been taken up with Finance Ministry so that the cost of production also comes clown. 
The Committee has noted that the following average production cost of sponge iron worked out 
in 1992:-
Gas based (old plants) Rs. 5102 per tonne 
Gas based (new plants) Rs. 5402 per tonne 
Coal based (old plants) Rs. 4150 per tonne 
Coal based (new plants) Rs. 5150 per tonne 
While clarifying the reasons for difference in production of new and old plants, the Secretary 
informed the Committee that old plants generally get fully depreciated and their fixed cost goes 
clown as a result of which cost of production becomes cheaper. On thf' ::::i1er hand the newer plants 
have got a heavy investment and their servicing cost is much higher which raises the cost of 
production. However, performance-wise new plants are better. 
5.8 ln the note furnished to the Committee the Ministry has informed that no study has been 
conducted to compare our production costs with production costs in other countries. The Secretary 
informed the Committee that as per the information available to them, sponge iron in the 
developed countries is generally produced for captive consumption. Information or data on 
international price of sponge iron is not even available with Sponge Iron Manufacturers' Association 
a~ nobody is importing spong iron from abroad, However. Government would make an attempt to 
conduct a study about it. About the quality of sponge iron of new plants the Secretary informed the 
Committee that the same is comparable to international level because of availability of good quality 
iron ore in the country. 
6.0 On the basis of the documents and other material made available and also the oral evidence 
of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel before it the Committee notes that rhe manufacturing 
process of the sponge iron has not been 'technologically sound and cost effective. The Committee 
has noted the requirement of high grade iron ore in sponge iron manufacturing process but good 
quality iron ore is not being extracted due to unscientific methods being used for this purpose. For 
example out of the total recoverable reserves of 76.1 million tonnes of iron ore in Goa only 13.5 
million tonnes is high grade and these deposits are rather scattered. The Committee feels that the 
available deposits of iron are in Goa are most valuable in terms of qual ity and if the same are 
extracted in a more scien tific way dependence in terms of import could be reduced to some extent. 
Though expensive but there is possibility of extracting iron ore of good qual ity in Goa by tak ing out 
the water out of the deposites which have otherwise remained unexplored clue to water level. 
The Committee observes that import of non-coking coal has been quite expensive. No serious 
efforts have been undertaken so far to ensure availability of good quality coal for sponge iron sector 
from the coal reserves available within the country and this had Jed to dependence on imports. The 
Commitree feels that the Ministry of Steel should urgently take up the matter with the Ministry of 
Coal so that good quality coal is made available to sponge iron industry at cheaper rates 
indigenously. 'Alternatively it would be cheaper if only coa l is imported and the non-coking process 
of the same is done in the country itself. The Committee expresses its concern over slackness and 
indifferent attitude of Government in not allotting gas to sponge iron industry despite the fact that 
sponge iron is included in the list of "High Priority Industries" in the new Ind ustrial Policy. The 

Committee is not convinced with Ministry's plea about non-availability of the same. The Committee 
feels that a lot of natural gas which is wasted everyday by way of flaring up could be utilised by 
allocating to sponge iron sector. Needful pursuasion with the Petroleum Ministry should be initiated 
in this direction. The Committee recommends that immediate steps be taken by the Ministry in 
getting the allocation of required natural gas to sponge iron industry for better productivity on the 
lines of power and fertilizer sectors. Implementation of certain units I projects would otherwise be 
jeopardisecl due to delay in supply of natural gas which will be a national Loss. 
6.1 The Committee is not satisfied with the growth of sponge iron production in the country. 
As per Government's own submission the production has been far below the installed capacity in 
most of the coal as well as gas based plants. The Committee feels that crucial areas like supply of 
better quality of coal and transportation of iron ore have been neglected to a large extent. Such lack 
of proper monitoring and feed back bas resulted into less capacity utilisation of the plants. The 
Committee is particularly not happy with the actual production figures in respect of Sponge Iron 
India Limited which is a PSU where the production has not reached the expected level despite of 
Government's efforts since the installation of the unit. The company has not only failed in achieving 
the production target but its performance in generating its internal resources has also been far from 
satisfactory during 1992-93 in comparison to 1991-92. The Company is thus in urgent need of 
protection in terms of supply of good quality of coal and favourable transportation conditions of 
iron for maintaining its viability. The Committee is not convinced with the Government's steps for 
achieving the proposed production targets of 6 million tonnes of sponge iron as projected at the end 
of Ylllth Five Year Plan. The Committee feels that the Ministry has no clear cut perception in 
achieving the target as no investment is proposed to be made by Government during the current 
plan and the entire additional capacity is expected to be set up in the private sector. The 
Government have downgraded its priorities towards the sponge iron industry by conceding the fact 
that it has no information about expansion of capacity utilisation being undertaken, if any, by 
private units. The Committee notes that Government have failed to intimate the Committee about 
the definite proposals which have come from the private sector which may enhance the production 
of sponge iron in future . The Committee observes that Government has by doing so left much to be 
desired by staking its claim for achieving the projected production target either in the absence of 
any Government investment or definite private proposals about setting new plants during VII Ith 
Plan period. The Committee therefore , recommends that Government should review its production 
targets and reschedule its priorities as per the available infrastructure vis-a-vis planning on ground 
realities. 
6.2 In the present conditions private enterpreneurs have a major role to play in contributing 
towards growth of sponge iron production in the country and a time has come when suitable 
package of incentives be given to them. The Committee has noted that as per present procedure an 
industrialist who wishes to set up a plant is required to fill up an Industrial Enterprenuer . 
Memorandum which is processed by a Linkage Committee in the Ministry. The Committee finds 
that follow up of the proposal is left to the enterpreneur. A system is required to be devised in the 
Ministry where the processing of private proposals could be expedited with constant and proper 
coordination with the concerned authorities and regular intraction with the enterpreneur should be 
maintained till a final decision is taken on his proposal. The Committee impresses upon the 
Government to immed iately process the proposals pending before it and devise an effective 
mechanism for their time bound implementation. 
6.3 The Committee is conscious about the factors responsible for increase in the production 
cost of sponge iron. It has been given to understand that the cost of production of sponge iron with 
present duty structure is very high. Suggestions of the manufacturers regarding reduction of customs 
duty on iron ore, iron ore pellets and non-coking coal are pending for clearance with Ministry of 
Finance. The Committee feels that the import duty of 35% on sponge iron is on the high side. This 
has increased a great burden on the sponge iron producers who have passed the same to the 

consumers by incre asing the prices five times since the last budger. This rising trend of prices would 
severely affect the industry as a whole . The Committee feels that budget relief annoui1ced this year 
have passed neither to the manufacturers nor the consumers. Consequently the steel industry in 
general and spon gl.! iron sector in particular is at the brink of disaster due to discriminatory 
approach of the Government. The Committee recommends that urgent remedial steps should be 
taken to revive the units I plants which have become sick and also those likely to be affected and 
appropriate duty reli"ef be given to the industry. 
6.4 The Committee finds that the no study has been conducted by Government to compare our 
production costs with production costs in other countries. The Committee is unhappy to note that 
such information is not available with any of the manufacturers. The Committee takes a serious 
note of such lack of foresightedness and initiative particularly in the present juncture when the 
country is to go global and accelerate the process of liberlisation and the required information could 
be more effect ive in the world scenerio. The Committee would like Government to conduct a 
comparative study of production cost of sponge iron in other countries so that the same could be a 
guiding factor while projecting <I balanced and well planned approach in arresting the rising cost of 
indigenous production on the basis of the experience of other wuntries in the matter. 
6.5 The Committee reitrates its concern for the urgent need for promotion of sponge iron 
industry , which has to play a vital role in secondary sector of steel production in the country. There 
is much scope for improvement in the planning so as to ensure capacity utilisation. The Committee 
is confident that practical and result oriented mechanism would be adopted by Government keeping 
in view the fact that the industry is exposed to favourable and positive options under the new 
Industrial Policy and it is included as ''High Priority Areas". If not given the requ ired protection at 
the juncture, the Committee foresees a bleak future for the industry which would be a tremendous 
national loss to economic regeneration and industrial growth. 
6.6 The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations as mentioned above will 
receive serious consideration for implementation.

3.2 Replying to the Commi"ee's query regarding the extent of participation of private 
enterpr ise into Non-Ferrous Mrning and Metallu rgical Industries and steps being taken to 
promote foreign investment. the Ministry of Mines stated tltat the Indian Mining Sector was 
opened up in stages. to private. including foreign investment, as part of the structural adju'>lntcnt 
programme of the Indian economy. This has been done in tune with the gen~ral economic 
libcralisation and reforms introduced by the Government in various sectors. The Nauonal 
Mineral Policy, 1993, enunciated this policy of encouraging private. including foreign investment 
in the mineral sector. The Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957, the ba_sic

statute, was amended in 1994, by which foreign direct investment (FDI) in the mineral sector was 
welcomed for the first time. Recently, in January, 2000, it has been further amended to grant 
greater security of tenure , and to simplify procedures, etc. so that the mining regime in India 
today is on par with global standards in this regard . 
3.3 The Central Government has const ituted the foreign Investment Promotion Board (FlPB) 
for clearance of applications for the foreign direct investment proposals. Since January 199\ the 
Government had been ,allowing FDI upto 50% in mining (except in respect of mining gold, silver 
and precious stones) and 74% in metallurb'Y and minera l processing through the automatic route. 
For FDI above these limits, the proposals had to come before the FIPB which used to consider 
them on a case to case basis. The FDI policy has been further liberalised w.e.f. ll 'h February , 
2000 to accelerate foreign investment in the mineral sector There will henceforth be no difference 
in tbe caps on foreign equity holdings to be allowed at ihe stages of exploration and that of 
mining:-
(a) For all minerals with which the Ministry of Mines is concerned other than diamonds 
& precious stones , foreign equ ity holding up to J 00% is allowed on the automatic 
route, for both explorat ion and mining. 
(b) In case of diamonds & precious stones, foreign equity up to 74% is allowed on the 
automatic route for both explora tion and mining operations. For proposals seeking 
higher than 74% foreign equity, the cases will have to come to FJPB for clearance. 
(c) Foreign equity upto 100% is allowed on the automatic route for processing of 
minerals and metallurgy . 
(d) There is no requirement of NOC from an exist ing joint venture partner for fresh 
investments . The prospective investo r will only have to give a declaration that he has 
no existingjoint venture for the same area and/or the partic~ar mineral.

17.1 The Committee observed that non-issuance of environmenta l clearance has become a 
big problem for mrning operators . The Minir\g lease is not executed until and unless 
environmen tal clearance is received . The Committee was informed that for mining areas 
over five hectares, environment clearance is neede~ . After getting the mining lease , the 
State Government asks the applicant to apply for forest clearance . Before granting 
environmental clearance. public hearing is also necessary . It takes minimum six months. In 
the case of non-schedule minerals , where the case does not come to the Centra l Government, 
the State government process the mining lease application and ask the party to g,et the

paid up capital of Rs. 50.00 lakh the accumulated loss till 31 .3.2000 stood at Rs. 189 crores. It 
has various problems like demand constraints. excessive manpower. financial constraints.

Government assistance in the form of Plan Loan, Non-Plan Loan, Grant-in-Aid for VRS etc. on 
consideration that mines are located in the backward region and most of the employees of BSLC 
belong to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Categories. If this Company is c l o~d down. 
there rna) be socio-economic problems in that region. The Board of Directors of the com pan). 
after detailed examination of the situation prevailing in BSLC suggested some alternatives as 
regards the future of the company. A meeting was held under the Chairmanship of Minister of 
Steel on 8.9.2000 to consider these alternatives. It was decided that some concrete steps i.e 
Reduction of manpo\\er from 1742 to 1300 by March, 200 I: Non revision of wages: and Off­
take of about 65000 tonnes of dolomite ·per month by SAIL Steel Plants should be taken to 
improve the Company's viability . The Ministry of Mines further stated that it is hoped that with 
these measures the Company would manage to raise enough resources to pay off its statutory 
dues and will not have to depend on Gover:nment of India for non-plan assistance.
