REDUCTION OF PLAN OUTLAY AT R.E. STAGE
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry should visualize the pros and cons of schemes before earmarking
funds.  Allocation of funds should be made depending on feasibility of scheme only.
 
 
COMMENTS
 
            This is correlated to Para 2.3, which pertains to the concern of the Committee regarding reduction in plan outlay at RE
stage. In this connection it is pertinent to note that BE and RE were same for SIDO for the year 2000-2001.However committee’s
observation has been noted.  The Working Group on Tenth Plan is also engaged in the task of recommending appropriate schemes
for the SSI Sector after taking into account the changed domestic and global scenario and also the targeted growth rate.
 
 
 
OFFICE OF DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER FOR
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Office of DC (SSI) which is also known as Small Industries Development Organisation is an apex body of the Ministry
and its role has increased to a great extent after the lifting of quantitative restrictions.  The Committee feels that the office of DC
should help the Small Scale Sector in evolving marketing strategies.  To help SSI sector, it should have well equipped computer
network for dissemination of information to that sector.  Technological upgradation is another area where its help to Small Scale
Sector is needed most and the office of DC should play a key role in improving the quality of the products of the SSI sector. 
Therefore, the office of DC needs to be further strengthened and, if necessary, its present allocation may be revised.
 
COMMENTS
 
            In order to strengthen the Office of DC (SSI), its Plan outlay has been enhanced from Rs. 266.50 crore in 1999-2000 to Rs.
379.55 crore in 2000-01 and further to Rs. 390.44 crore in 2001-2002. The Office has taken measures to enable the SSI Sector to
face the challenges after the removal of Quantitative Restrictions. Steps taken for providing market support include formulation of
SSI Exporters Market Development Assistance (SSI – MDA) Scheme to encourage the efforts of SSI Exporters in tapping and
developing overseas markets, organising Vendor Development Programmes–cum–Buyer–Seller–Meets and Exhibitions at different
locations all over the country, conducting Training  Programmes on Packaging for exports to acquaint SSI exporters with the latest
packaging techniques/standards, reservation of 358 items exclusively for purchases from Small Scale Sector under the Government
Stores Purchase Programme and  constitution of a sub-group on marketing and export for SSI Sector under the Chairmanship of
CMD, NSIC.
 
For Technology upgradation the following measures have been taken up:
 
Ø
      A Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation was operationalised with effect from  1st
October, 2000  wherein 12% back ended Capital Subsidy is admissible on loans advanced  to small scale industries by
the scheduled commercial banks/designated SFCs for technology upgradation in select products/sub-products of known 
proven technologies.
 
Ø
      The office of DC(SSI) has introduced an incentive scheme of ISO-9000 certification, which aims at encouraging
technology upgradation and quality improvement in the SSI Sector and preparing it to face the global competition. The
scheme provides reimbursement of 70% of the amount spent for acquiring ISO 9000 certification(or its equivalent) upto
Rs. 75,000 to each SSI Unit. The Scheme has been in operation since March,1994 and 1384 cases have been reimbursed
upto 31.3.2001.The government has extented the scheme till the end of the 10
th Five Year Plan. The office of DC(SSI)
has simultaneously taken up Awareness & Motivational Programme on ISO 9000 and TQM Quality Systems.
 
Ø      Setting up of Incubation Centres in Sunrise Industries-The Secretaries of Ministries/Departments dealing with  Sunrise
Industries have been requested to consider the setting up of Incubation Centres in their respective areas. A Budget
provision of Rs.10 lakh has also been kept for the financial year 2001-2002 to provide the assistance, if required, by
them.

SIDBI and NSIC.  NSIC’s compendium has been hosted on NSIC’s Web site.   SIDBI has recently prepared a

.

Moreover, to address the computerisation related needs of SIDO, a project called Small Enterprises Information & Resource
Centre Network (SENET) was started on Ist April, 1997. The project was revised in March, 2000 to include office automation and
web enabled applications with a total project cost of Rs.1140.38 lakh.  It functions with 5 Technology Nodal Centres and 15 User
Centres, spread all over the country.
 
The Prime objective of SENET is to facilitate the networking amongst the information providers and seekers (National /
State level Industries Associations, NGOs and the entrepreneurs) as well as Central/ State Governments, other Central/ State
agencies engaged directly or indirectly in the promotion and development of the small scale sector.  The data base created by
SENET regarding investment opportunities in the country etc. will be put on world wide web (Internet) to facilitate global access
and making the website accessible by the entrepreneurs 24 hours (round the clock).
 
Further, the Ministry has recently launched its portal on SSI, which not only gives updated online information on
policies/programmes of the Ministry, but also provides links to other related web-sites.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4.4
 
NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
            The  Committee observes that the Government is not providing financial assistance to the NSIC in the form of equity. 
NSIC is projected to generate Rs. 120.00 crore in budget 2000-01.  Devoid of equity support, NSIC would be hard pressed to
generate revenue on its own now.  The Committee therefore recommends that NSIC should take measures to increase IEBR and
explore ways and means for more revenue generation to become self sufficient.  Till NSIC becomes self reliant, the govt. may
continue to provide funds for the Corporation so that its development activities continue unabated.   
COMMENTS
 
            The Government continues to provide funds for the development activities. For the year 2001-2002, a plan budget of Rs. 29
crore has been provided to NSIC for Marketing Assistance, Development  of N.E. regions, Modernisation  programme, Exchange
variation losses and reimbursement of expenditure of NTSCs and Govt. purchases. A provision of Rs. 5.5 crore (Non Plan) has also
been made for NSIC for reimbursement of expenditure & Govt. purchases to NTSC Okhla, NTSC Rajkot and  NTSC Howrah.
            The Government had approved IEBR of Rs. 517.00 crore for the Corporation during the 9
th Plan period. During the first
four years of the 9th Plan period i.e. during 1997-98 to 2000-01, an amount of Rs. 478.91 crore has been raised by the Corporation
out of Rs. 517.00 crore proposed for the Ninth Five Year Plan.  Further NSIC has been given IEBR mobilisation target of Rs. 120
crore for 2000-2001. The NSIC has already been provided with an equity support of Rs. 58 crores during the Ninth Plan. Action on
enhancing the Equity support will be taken after considering the report of the Consultant appointed for the restructuring of the
NSIC.
 
 
OTHER SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES SCHEMES

RECOMMENDATIONS
           
The Committee hopes that the schemes viz. Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation, Integrated
Infrastructural Development Scheme, Technology Upgradation and collection of statistics etc. would be implemented successfully
and the targets fixed-both physical and financial would be achieved.  In view of lifting of Quantitative Restrictions, the time has
come to lay more emphasis on technological upgradation and modernisation.  For this purpose, if need be, allocation may be
increased.
 
COMMENTS
 
            The Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme has been recently operationalized by SIDBI (Nodal Agency) through scheduled
commercial banks/NSIC and an advance of Rs. 5.00 Crore has already been given to SIDBI last year. An outlay of Rs. 25 crore
exists for the current year. The progress of scheme would be closely monitored.  At present the scheme covers only 14 sub sectors
of SSI sector.  The scope and coverage of the scheme can be expanded by including more sub-sectors on the advice of Governing
Technology Advisory Board (GTAB) along with the enhancement of Budget provisions accordingly. 
 
            Under the UPTECH Scheme, 9 clusters of industries have been taken up for Modernisation and Technology Upgradation. In
addition, 2 National Programmes in collaboration with UNIDO have also been taken up. Funds allocated in RE for 2000-2001 for
UPTECH Scheme were stepped up considerably to give more emphasis on technology upgradation.
 
            The Integrated Infrastructure Development (IID) Scheme earlier covered backward districts/rural areas which were not
covered under the Growth Centres Scheme, being implemented by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion. The scope
of the scheme has now been extended by covering  all areas in the country.
 
Under the modified scheme  50 percent reservation has been provided for the rural areas and    the funds available  under
the non-lapsable  pool for the North East will be made use  of  for Industrial Infrastructure Development, setting up of incubation
centres, for cluster development and for setting up of IIDs in the North East including Sikkim.
 
Various components of the Plan Scheme “ Collection of Statistics  of SSI “ are progressing as per the targets. The monthly
data for Index of Industrial Production (IIP) are being collected, compiled and supplied to CSO every month. IIP for the SSI Sector
is being compiled every quarter as per the targets. Registration data received from every State/UT Directorate is being compiled
every quarter and data on commulative number of SSI units registered with the State Directorate of Industries (SDIs) are being

ANTI-DUMPING DUTY
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Committee observes that it takes 90 days to review economic fallout of imported goods in country and imposition of
anti-dumping duties thereon.  By that time huge financial losses would have already occurred to the country, which are
irretrievable.  The Committee observes that in order to preclude the possibility of economic losses, anti-dumping monitoring should
be expedited.  The Committee therefore recommends that the administrative ministry should review the pros and cons in this regard
and take timely action.  The system that exists in other countries may be examined.  India can also emulate such a system.
 
COMMENTS
The Anti-Dumping Authority in the Ministry of Commerce & Industry is fully geared up to decide any formal complaints of
dumping by any country expeditiously.  In view of the legitimate demand of the domestic industry to provide immediate relief in
the face of dumping faced by them, the Directorate General of Anti-dumping & Allied Duties (DGAD), has streamlined its process
of investigation and Preliminary Findings are now being issued within a period of two-and-a-half to three months from the date of
initiation as against over six months being taken in the previous years.
The DGAD also actively participated in the workshops/seminars in different parts of the country organized by Association
of Industries to disseminate information on anti-dumping laws and procedures and to facilitate the domestic industry in submitting
their properly documented petitions for initiation of cases. India is one of the leading users of Anti-Dumping  measures in the
world. As Per the WTO report of 2000 India was the most active member during the year 1999 in terms of initiation of Anti-
Dumping investigations followed by EU, USA, and Argentina. At the same time, the transparency and thoroughness of our
investigations is borne out by the fact that not a single case initiated by DGAD has been brought before the Dispute Settlement
Body by any of the exporting countries.  We have been using the anti-dumping mechanisms very effectively.
The Directorate takes approximately 3 months to bring the preliminary findings of an Anti-dumping initiation.  In terms of
time taken for issue of preliminary findings, India compares favourably with other important users of Anti-Dumping measures in
the world.
 
Country Average Time Taken
India Approx.3 months
USA Approx.4-5 months
EU Approx.7-8months
Australia Approx. 5 months
New Zealand Approx.5-6 months
 
 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Committee understands that enacting law in this matter is not the concern of this ministry.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the matter may be taken up with the concerned administrative ministry for making a law, if necessary.  Otherwise
necessary regulations may be prepared by the concerned Ministry and the Ministry of Small Scale Industries & Agro and Rural
Industries may pursue it.
 
COMMENTS

63rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/63rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:13:33]
The matter was taken up with Directorate General of Anti-dumping & Allied Duties(DGAD), Ministry of Commerce &
Industry, who have informed that the Designated Authority appointed by the Government conducts Anti-Dumping investigations in
India under Sections 9A, 9B and 9C of the Customs Tariff Act of 1975 as amended in 1995. According to the Anti-Dumping Rules
the initiation of Anti-Dumping investigations is undertaken when the domestic industry files a fully documented petition to the
Designated Authority with prima-facie evidence of dumping, injury and causal link between the dumping of the imported goods
and injury to the domestic industry. However, under the rule 5(4) of  the Customs Tariff Rules of 1995, the Designated Authority
may  initiate investigations suo-moto if it is satisfied with the information recevied from the Collector of Customs appointed under
the Customs Act, 1962 or from any other source that sufficient evidence exists regarding dumping of the foreign goods, material
injury to the domestic industry and causal link between the two.
Article VI of WTO Agreements prescribes the guidelines on Anti-Dumping measures to be followed by the member
countries for imposition of anti-dumping duties and countervailing duties. The guidelines are designed on the previous anti-
dumping code under Article VI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and states as to how the member countries
can invoke anti-dumping duties against another member country. The new guidelines inter-alia provide time limits for various
stages of investigations to be conducted, the methodology of determination of the extent of anti-dumping and the measures to be
adopted by the member countries.
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Committee feels that availability of imported commodities, relatively of cheap quality without carrying MRP and ISI
labels, poses a serious threat to the domestic industries, particularly the small scale sector.  The Government should look into this
matter on priority basis and take all appropriate measures to protect the interests of domestic industries from unfair competition
from imported goods.
 
COMMENTS
 
The Government is closely monitoring the imports and all necessary steps to safeguard the interests of the domestic industry
are being taken. A Notification has been issued by the Ministry of Commerce & Industry on 24.11.2000, regarding compliance of
all the conditions of the Standards of Weights and Measures (packaged commodity) Order, 1977, on imports as applicable to
domestic producers.  In addition, the importers of packaged commodities have to comply with the following conditions:
 
a)
      Name and address of the importer,
b)      Generic or common name of the commodity packed;
c)      Net quantity in terms of standard units of weights and measures, if the net quantity in the imported package is given to
any other unit, its equivalent in terms of standard units shall be declared by the importer;
d)      Month and year of packing in which the commodity is manufactured or packed or imported;
e)      Maximum retail sale  price (MRP) at which the commodity in packaged form may be sold to the ultimate consumer. 
This price shall include all taxes, local or otherwise, freight transport charges, commission payable to dealers and all
charges towards advertising, delivery, packing, forwarding and the like as the case may be.
 
The Notification also makes the import of 131 products subject to compliance with  the mandatory India quality standards
as applicable to  domestic goods.  For compliance of this requirement all manufacturers/ exporters of these products to India shall
be required to register themselves with the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).  The list of 131 products includes various food
preservatives and additives, milk powder, infant milk food, certain kinds of cement, household and similar electrical appliances and
multi-purpose dry batteries.

RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to bridge the gap between the sanctioned cases and actual
disbursal of loans under PMRY.  The Committee also recommends that the number of beneficiaries should be increased.  If
necessary, allocation may be increased at RE stage.
 
COMMENTS
 
As per the report received from the RBI, loans were sanctioned to 7,91,850 persons during the years 1997-98; 1998-99 and
1999-2000.  During the year 2000-01 loans were sanctioned to 2,29,437 persons and disbursed to 1,27,890 persons against the
target of 2,20,000 as reported by the RBI.  The figure for disbursement is likely to go up as the cut off date for completion of
disbursement has been stipulated as 31.12.2001.
 
            However, the RBI has been requested to issue necessary instructions to the implementing banks to speed up the process of
disbursement to bridge the gap between sanctions and disbursements.  The State/UTs have also been requested to arrange training
and other pre-disbursal formalities so that the gap between the sanctions and disbursement is reduced. 
 
            To ensure the achievement of plan target of 2,20,000 at national level, better performing States are allocated additional
target in addition to basic targets.  However, some States/UTs could not achieve the basic target due to various socio-economic
factors e.g. militancy and unstable political situation and due to reluctance on the part of banks to disburse loan on account of poor
recovery of loan overdues.  However, the RBI as well as the States/UTs have been requested to achieve the allocated target and
bridge the gap between sanctions and disbursement. 
 
Over and above the plan target of 2.20 lakh for 2001-2002 an additional target of 1.07 lakh have been allocated to better
performing States/UTs.  Due to the requirement of undergoing training and completion of pre-disbursement formalities, the loan for
the cases sanctioned in the year 2001-2002 may also be disbursed in 2002-2003. Depending upon the requirement of funds, the
Budget Estimate for 2002-2003 will be worked out.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
The Committee feels that there is a need to keep a constant vigil over the loan disbursement under  PMRY particularly on
the non-target achieving states. Before allocating  fresh target it should be ensured that the earlier target has been achieved.

disbursed and rejected with reasons therefor for the year 2001-2002.

RECOMMENDATIONS
 
 
            The Committee recommends that the policy package for credit guarantee scheme may be made operational at the earliest in
case it has not been made as yet.  The Committee also feels that the lengthy bureaucratic red tapism in clearing credit needs to be
removed and rules be simplified and made easy.
 
COMMENTS
 
            Credit Guarantee Scheme has been launched in August, 2000 to provide guarantee for loans upto Rs.25 lakh  extended by
the commercial banks, selected well performing Regional Rural Banks and other Financial Institutions  without any collateral 
including third party guarantee.  A Credit Guarantee Fund Trust of SIDBI (CGTSI) has been created to implement the Scheme.   18
Scheduled Commercial Bank, 1 Regional Rural Bank, National Small Industries Corporation and North Eastern Development
Finance Corporation have registered with CGTSI as Member Lending Institutions for availing guarantee facility. Upto July, 2001, 
2009 cases have been sanctioned with guarantee cover extended for an aggregate credit of Rs. 12.86 crore.
 
            The application forms for loans have been  simplified based on the recommendations of the Nayak Committee.
Computation of credit needs has also been made simple by computing it on the basis of 20% of the projected annual turnover upto a
borrowal limit of Rs.5 crore. As per the extant guidelines, application for credit limits up to Rs. 25000, is to be disposed of within a
fortnight and those for loans beyond Rs.25000 within 8 to 9 weeks. The recommendation of Study Group on Development of Small
Scale Enterprises (Dr S.P.Gupta Committee) that loan applications up to Rs 5 Lakh may be disposed within a month, is under
consideration.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS
 
            The Committee feels that the  S.P. Gupta  Committee recommendation on fast processing of loan applications be  dealt on a
priority  basis and an early decision be taken.

availing guarantee facility. The Committee recommends that SIDBI should ensure that all the Public Sector banks should register
with it for the purpose.

            The Committee recommends that the tax – exempt status as provided in the Small Industries Development Bank of India

             The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance to restore the tax-exempt status of SIDBI as before. In their
reply, Ministry of Finance has mentioned that a conscious policy decision was taken to remove Section 50 of SIDBI Act which
pertains to income tax exemption available to SIDBI. This decision has been taken in view of the fact that the institution is in
existence for a  considerable period now and has been working on commercial basis, therefore, there is no rationale for retaining
tax exemption while similar institutions are paying their taxes.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS
 
The Committee understands that the concessional resource support available to SIDBI            in earlier years from
Government of India/RBI have gradually depleted. By this, SIDBI has been forced to approach open market for mobilizing
resource requirements. The Committee has also been given to understand that expectations from various quarters for investment by

INDO-NEPAL TRADE TREATY
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
The Committee would like the Ministry to look into this aspect of unfair competition being posed by the imports from
Nepal. The Committee understands that the Indo-Nepal Trade Treaty is due for review during the later part of 2001. It would,
therefore, recommend that this matter may be looked into and corrective measures taken.
 
COMMENTS
 
            Import from Nepal is governed by the  Indo-Nepal Treaty on Trade and Transit. The Indo-Nepal Treaty was last amended in
December, 1996 and is valid upto 5
th December, 2001. The Treaty will be automatically renewed in the normal course if either side
gives no notice. During the last amendment in December, 1996, the existing value addition norms were deleted and all products
manufactured in Nepal were eligible for duty free exports to India.  In the absence of value addition norms there has been a rapid
growth of imports into India of some Nepalese commodities. This has led to representations from domestic industries in these
sectors. Representations have been received regarding excessive import of many products. The industry has pointed out that in
absence of proper  rules of origin, Nepal has become a re-export point for many of the products from China and other South Asian
countries. The provision of certificate of origin was dispensed with in the new treaty. This has given rise to a spurt in flow of
Chinese goods in the guise of Nepalese goods which has badly affected the Indian industry particularly small scale and medium
industry as they are unable to compete with the cheap Chinese goods which are coming via Nepal.
 
            The Indo-Nepal Treaty is due for review shortly and these concerns can be addressed at the time of review. In the best
interest of Indian Trade and Industry it is essential now to review the Indo-Nepal Treaty, making it mandatory for goods
manufactured in Nepal to be accompanied by the certificate of origin and prescribing value addition norms. Nepal's accession to
WTO is also to be negotiated shortly and these issues of Indian concerns can also be taken up at that time.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
            The Committee hopes that the anomalies arising out of Indo-Nepal treaty in the new scenario would be addressed to and
concrete measures would be taken to redress the grievances of Indian manufacturers at the time of review of the treaty.

REPORT
 
            The Offshore Areas Mineral (Development And Regulation) Bill, 2001 was referred to the Committee on
Industry by the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on  7
th September, 2001 under  Rule 270(b) of the Rules of Procedure
and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha for examination and report thereon.
2          The Bill aims to provide for development and regulation of mineral resources in the territorial  waters,
continental shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India and   to provide  for matters connected
therewith or incidental  thereto.
3          According to   the statement of objects and reasons of the Bill, the need was felt to have  proper legal   frame
work for   regulation and  development of minerals occurring  in the offshore areas, that is,  territorial waters,
continental shelf, exclusive  economic zone and other maritime zones of  India, in order to develop the offshore  areas
scientifically and  systematically.   India  has approximately 3.3 million square kilometres  of land area  with a coast line
of 8041 kilometres. The area of the Exclusive Economic Zone is 2.02 million square kilometres and  in terms of the UN
Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982,  the coastal states have specific rights and jurisdiction, inter alia,  for exploring
and exploiting the natural resources over the continental margin, which will add about 0.80 million square kilometres in
addition to the area of Exclusive Economic Zone. In  India, beach placer deposits have been economically exploited
since long. The mining and processing of different minerals obtained from these placer deposits into valuable products

are also well established. India is richly endowed in mineral sands in the Eastern and Western Coasts. Heavy mineral
sand containing mostly  ilmenite with some rutile, leucoxene (a decomposition product of ilmenite), garnet, zircon,
monazite and aluminium silicates like silimanite and kyanite occur in isolated to extensive spreads all along the sea
coast.
4          The proposed legislation would enable streamlining of mineral exploration and development in the offshore
areas and ensure systematic and scientific exploitation of mineral reserves (except petroleum, natural gas and
hydrocarbon resources) for attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
5.         Under the Law of the Sea  convention, 1982, the coastal states   are  entitled to territorial sea (12 nautical miles), 
contiguous zone (24 nautical miles) exclusive  economic zone (200 nautical miles) and   continental shelf (200/350
nautical  miles) drawn from normal base-line, which is the low-water line along  the coast,  over which the  coastal
States have specific rights and Jurisdiction, including for  exploring and  exploiting the natural  resources.  The
Convention   came into effect  on 16
th November, 1994 and became part of the  International Law, India has ratified the
Law of the Sea Convention on  29th June, 1995.  Article  297 of the Constitution of India was amended by the  40th
Amendment to the Constitution and according to amended Article 297 , all lands , minerals and other things of value
underlying the  ocean within the   territorial water, or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone of  India, 
shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes  of the Union.  In 1976, the Parliament passed the Territorial
Waters, Continental Shelf , Exclusive  Economic zone and other Maritime Zones Bill, 1976 delineating therein the
limits of the zones and rights and obligations in maritime zones.
6.         Entry  54 of   List-I of the Constitution gives powers to the Central Government for regulation of mines and
mineral development to the extent to which such regulation and  development under the control of the   Union is
declared by  Parliament by law to be  expedient in the public interest.  The Bill has been introduced accordingly. 
Further, the  clauses 16 and 17 of the Bill provide that royalty and fixed rent shall be payable to the Central Government
and, therefore, in accordance with Article 117 (1) of the  Constitution of India, which requires  that any Bill making
provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f)   of clause (1)  of article110   [Definition of   "Money
Bills."] ,  recommendation of the President has been obtained prior to introduction of the Bill.
7.         As per amendments  made  on November, 10, 1992 to the  Allocation of  Business Rules,  1961, legislation for
regulation  of mines and development of minerals underlying  the ocean within the territorial waters, or the continental 
shelf of the exclusive   economic zone and other maritime   zones of India has been placed under the charge of the
Department of Mines.  In May,.  1993 a working group was constituted, headed  by the Joint Secretary, Department of
Mines, for finalising the legislation for offshore areas .  Terms of reference of the working group were  (i) to suggest a
suitable legislation and rules for regulating prospecting and mining in the  Territorial Waters, c Continental Shelf and
Exclusive Economic Zone of India after examining the existing legislation of the  subject viz.  the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957  (MMDR Act) , and the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive
Economic Zone and other Maritime Zone Act, 1976 and other related matters; and (ii) to make any  other
recommendations as may be considered necessary.  The working group    has taken into consideration the opinion
expressed  by Ministry of Law, ( January, 1974) that if, by virtue of special requirement of minerals in the offshore
areas, it is considered necessary to lay down conditions or restriction which are at variance with the existing statutory
provisions in the MMDR Act, 1957 , then under such circumstances, it would not be legally permissible to do  so
without first   amending the statute, i.e. MMDR Act, 1957  itself suitably.  It was  also observed that by virtue of Article
297 of the Constitution, the ownership of minerals in the offshore areas vests  in the Union and if the MMDR Act were
to be used for  framing rules applicable to offshore areas  it would require extensive amendments.   The Wording Group
also  examined the possibility of framing Rules under section 15 of the Maritime Zone act, 1976.  It was observed 
however, that the Maritime Zones  Act   is in the nature of umbrella legislation and if Rules are to be framed under this
Act, provisions normally included  in the Act will   have to  be  necessarily provided for in the Rules,   This  could be a
doubtful course of action, as it would amount to "excessive delegation"  through the rules which is not desirable in  any 
legislation.  The Working  Group, therefore, came to the conclusion that it would be advisable to frame a new Act for
mineral exploitation in offshore areas and submitted its report and draft of the proposed legislation accordingly in
December, 1995.   The Report and the proposed draft legislation was further examined in  extensive consultation with
all Departments and Ministries in the Government of India who have  stakes in off shore areas.  Accordingly the Bill has
been prepared, duly addressing the concerns of all stake holders.
8.         The Bill consists of   38 clauses spreading over six chapters  and two schedules .  Chapter-I of the proposed
legislation, i.e. Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Bill consists of first   4 Clauses of the Bill giving
details of  short title and commencement, Declaration  as to  expediency of Union control, Application, Definitions.

8.1       Clause-1 of the chapter -I gives preliminary information such  as : short title, extent and commencement, Clause-
2   contains   declaration as to expediency of Union to take under its control the regulation of the mines and
development of minerals in offshore areas to enable Parliament to enact the proposed legislation.   Clauses-3 species 
that the proposed legislation shall apply to all minerals in offshore areas except mineral oils and hydrocarbons and the
provisions of the  proposed legislation shall be in addition to and not in derogation of any other law for the  time being
in  force in the offshore areas.  This would  ensure that the strategic and defence  interests of the country are fully
safeguarded.   Clause -4   contains  the definitions in the proposed legislation, which, inter-alia, includes definitions like 
`administering authority', `exploration licence,   `exploration operations',  `mine',   `off shore areas',  `pollution of
offshore environment', `production lease', reconnaissance operation', reconnaissance permit etc. In the proposed
legislation  there would be three types of operating rights,  namely reconnaissance permit (non exclusive), exploration
licence and production lease. Clause 4 (v)  states that  reconnaissance permit means a permit granted under section 11
for the purpose of undertaking reconnaissance operation.  While  the production  lease means   a lease granted  under
section 13 which confers an exclusive right for the purpose of undertaking production operation.   Production operation
means any operation undertaken for the purpose of winning any mineral from the offshore area and includes any
operation directly or indirectly necessary therefor or incidental thereto.  Clause 4 (u) states reconnaissance operation
means any  preliminary geo-scientific  survey undertaken for the purpose of searching or locating mineral deposits.
8.2.      Chapter-II deals with  General Provisions for Acquisition of  Operating Rights in the Offshore Areas.  Clause 5,
provides that no person shall undertake any reconnaissance operation,  exploration operation or production   operation 
in the  offshore areas except under and in accordance  with the prescribed terms and conditions of the  reconnaissance 
permit,  exploration licence  or production lease granted under  the proposed legislation and the rules made thereunder. 
The clause also enables agencies of the  Central Government  including the  Geological Survey of India, Atomic
Mineral Directorate of Exploration and Research, Naval Hydrographic office, National Institute of  oceanography and
the  National Institute  of  Ocean Technology to carry out  reconnaissance  and  exploration operations without requiring
a permit or license  under the proposed  legislation.  This clause lays down the various requirements  regarding
dissemination of the data generated which the  permitee or licensee  or a lessee has to furnish   and also seeks to
empower the  Central Government to provide for  special measures as may be required for seaward artillery practice  ,
ensuring public safety and interest, defence of India and civil defence , conduct of naval operations and exercises,
national   security and other strategic  considerations.  This clause further ensures that scientific research carried out by
the Central Government  agencies is not fettered by the proposed legislation.

obtained from these  placer   deposits into valuable products are also well established.  India is richy endowed  in
mineral sands on the Eastern and Western Coasts.  Heavy mineral sands containing mostly  ilmenite with some ruitile,
leucoene (a decomposition product of limenite), garnet, zircon, monazite and aluminium silicates like sillimanite and
kyanite occur in isolated  to extensive spreads all along the Indian sea coasts.
2.         During the course of  oral evidence the Department of Mines  informed the Committee  that  the Geological
Survey of India  (Marine Wing) undertakes sea-bed survey within the  Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) of India  for
non-living  resources and investigation relating to the earth-science.  During the   course of survey, Geological Survey
of India have delineated heavy mineral  sands comprising  ilmenite,  rutile, zicon, Silimanite monazite and granite off
the cost of Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka; phosphatised sedimentary  in water depths  of 200-1000
meters off Gujarat coast , high grade lime mud deposit in water  depths of 180-1200 meters off Gujarat coast, Oolites
and  calcareous sands in water depth of 50-200 meters of Maharashtra and  Gujarat Coasts, high grade  lime mud
deposit in  water  depths of 100-200 meters of Andhra coasts, phosphatised sediments in  water  depths of 100-200
meters  South east of  Chennai, Micro manganese nodules in water depth of  2800-4300  meters in Lakshadweep Sea,
high grade calcareous sands in shallow offshore and lagoons  of Lakshadweep  and  calcareous sediments in water
depths of 1000 meter west of  Andaman and  Nicobar  Group of   Islands. As per the preliminary  survey done by the
Geological Survey of India, the minerals which are likely to be found include ilmenite with some rutile, leucoxena ( a
decomposition product of ilmenite), granite , zircon, monazite, aluminium silicates like sillimanite and  kyanite, micro
manganese nodule, lime mud phosphates, etc. Under the legislation, however, all the minerals are being covered.
3.         The Committee was given to  understand  that  the   need to have a proper legal framework for regulation and
development of  minerals  occurring  in the offshore areas. i.e. territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic
zone and other maritime zones of India. Replying to the Committee's  query  whether  the existing  legal framework on
the subject viz.  the Mines and Minerals ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) and the Territorial
Waters, Continental Shelf, exclusive Economic Zone and other  Maritime Zone Act, 1976 proved  deficient for making
rules for  development of offshore areas in a scientific and  systematic manner so much so that the need of separate  and
fresh legislation was felt the Department of Mines  stated that  in May 1993 a working group  was constituted  headed
by the Joint Secretary, Department of  Mines for finalizing the legislation for offshore areas.  The working group was 
asked  to suggest  a suitable legislation and rules  for  regulating, prospecting  and mining in the  territorial waters,
continental shelf AND EEZ  of  India after examining the existing legislation on the  subject, namely,  the Mines and
Minerals  ( Regulation and Development) Act,  1957 , the  Territorial Waters, Continental  Shelf, Exclusive Economic
Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 and other related matters.     The  Ministry  of Law  had advised that  if by
virtue of  special requirements  of minerals in the  offshore areas, it is considered necessary to lay down  conditions or
restrictions which are at variance with the existing statutory provisions in  the MMDR Act, 1957, then under such
circumstances, it would not be legally permissible to do so without first  amending the Principal Act.  The features 
unique to development of mineral resources in  the offshore   areas  were different    in the environment, the nature of
operations and  the equipments required and hence it was  felt  that rules framed under the MMDR Act would   not be 
adequate in  the matter. The other possibility was framing rules under   section 15 of the Territorial  Waters, Continental
Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones   Act, 1976.  Maritime Zones Act is in the nature of
umbrella legislation and  therefore if rules were to be framed under this Act, the provisions normally  included in the
Act were to be necessarily provided for in the  rules.  This could be  a doubtful course of action, as it would amount to
excessive delegation through  rules.  Accordingly, therefore, the Working Group came to the conclusion that it would
be  advisable to   frame a new  Act  for mineral exploitation in Offshore areas, which has  formed the  basis of the
Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Bill.    Further more the purpose of the Territorial Waters,
Continental Shelfs, Exclusive Economic Zones and other Maritime  Zone Act, 1976 is  mainly to define  and determine
the limit of the territorial water continental  shelf, exclusive    economic zone and other maritime zone of India and to
regulate certain other  limited matters relating to them.  The said Act   does  not specifically provides for  grant of
reconnaissance permit exploration license  or production lease  for the  purposes  of  extracting minerals from sea land. 
The Mines and Minerals  ( Development and Regulation) act, 1957 was enacted mainly for  the purpose of development
and regulation of mines and minerals under the  land only.  It was  not intended to regulate and develop the mines and
minerals in the offshore  areas.  The development and regulation of mineral resources in the  territorial water,
continental shelfs, exclusive economic zones and other maritime zones  need a different expertise, technical ability  and
separate methodology of operation performed or carried out by the use of vessel, erection, appliance, artificial island
and platforms, etc.  The measurement of wave tides, hydrography etc.  are required   for which separate conditions of
licenses and permits are  required to regulate the licenses, permits and leases of quite different nature   specifically for

the purpose of offshore areas.   The  specific provision by way of the Offshore  Areas  Mineral ( Development and
Regulation) Bill, 2001 are required  to regulate the exploration and production  of mines and minerals in  offshore  areas
which  are not contained in Mines  and Minerals (  Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.  The  provisions of the Bill
as provided  in clause 3 (2)  thereof are in addition to and not in derogation of any other law for the time being  in force. 
As such, the provisions are within the  frame work of the existing  legislation and do  not put any hindrance in the
administration of other enactments.   The representatives of  the Legislative  Department  endorsed the view point of 
the Department of Mines .   
4.         The  Committee feels that in order to develop the offshore areas scientifically and systematically it is pertinent to
have a proper legal frame-work for regulation and development of minerals occurring in the offshore areas, that is,
territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India. The proposed
legislation would enable streamlining of mineral exploration and development in the offshore areas and ensure
systematic and scientific exploitation of mineral reserves (except petroleum, natural gas and hydrocarbon resources) for
attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
5.         The Committee  observe  that  under the law of the sea convention, 1982 , the coastal states  are entitled to
territorial sea (12 nautical miles), contiguous zone (24 nautical miles) exclusive economic zone (200 nautical miles) and
continental shelf (200/350  nautical miles) drawn from normal base-line, which is the low-water line along the coast,
over which the coastal States have specific   rights and Jurisdiction, including for exploring and exploiting the natural  
resources.  The Conventional came into effect on 16
th November, 1994 and became part of the International Law,  India
has ratified the Law  of the Sea Convention on 29th June, 1995.  The Department of  Mines  informed the Committee
that   Article 297  of the Constitution of   India was amended by the 40th Amendment to the Constitution and according
to amended Article 297, all lands, minerals and other things of  value  underlying the ocean within the territorial water,
or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone of  India,  shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes
of the Union.  In 1976, the  Parliament passed the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic  Zone and
other  maritime zones  Act, 1976 delineating therein  in the limit of the zones and  rights and obligations in maritime
zones.  Entry 54 of List-I of  the Constitution gives powers to the Central Government for  regulation of mines and
mineral development to the  extent to which such regulation and development under the control of the Union is declared
by Parliament by  law to be expedient in the public interest.  The Bill has been introduced accordingly.
6.         The Committee is of the  view  that  the proposed legislation  have sufficient legal  frame-work for making rules
necessary for development and regulation of offshore areas . Some of highlights which  takes care of all required legal-
framework  are as follows: —
There will be three types of operating rights, namely, Reconnaissance permit (non exclusive), exploration licence and
production lease.
The offshore areas will be released periodically for grant of operating rights only after inter-departmental consultation
with the Ministries/Departments  which have parallel interest in the offshore areas.
Exploration licence or production lease will be granted to any person over an area only upon submission of a work
programme for the exploration operation, or development of the mineral deposits in that area. This would ensure that
exploration and mining operations in the offshore areas are conducted on a scientific basis with due regard to
conservation.
No operating right shall be granted to any person unless such  person is an Indian national or a company as defined in
sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956).
The holder of the reconnaissance  permit shall commence work within a period of six months, the holder of the
exploration licence shall commence work within a period of one year and the holder of the production lease shall
commence commercial production within a period of two years from the date of grant.
Reconnaissance permit will be granted for a maximum period of two years with the provision for renewal for another
maximum period of two years. Exploration licence shall be granted initially for a  maximum period of three years with a
provision for renewal so that the total period of exploration does not exceed five years. Production lease shall be granted
initially for a period not exceeding thirty years with the provision for renewal for twenty years.
The Central Government is being authorised by notification in the Official  Gazette to prescribe norms for the safety and
health of persons and safety and security of  property in offshore areas.
There is a provision  for payment of royalty and in order to discourage the speculative acquisition of large areas, there 
is also  provision for payment of fixed rent. The rate will be prescribed by notification, with the proviso that  royalty and
fixed rent shall not be enhanced more than once during any period of three years.
In order to safeguard defence and security of the country,  the provisions of the proposed legislation shall be in addition

to and not in derogation of any other law for the time being in force in the offshore areas.
There is  an enabling clause for making rules to address problems of pollution of offshore environment and security and
safety of marine life including fin and shell fish, coral and other species. Every holder of the operating rights shall be
liable for any pollution or damage to marine environment resulting from  activities in the offshore areas.
7.         The Committee notes and endorses the contention  of the Department of Mines  that  the proposed  legislation  
would be able to  provide  for regulation and development of mineral resources in the territorial waters, continental
shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India  and to provide for matters connected therewith or
incidental thereto.  The Bill when enacted would help in streamlining mineral exploration and development in the
offshore areas for attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
8.         The Committee is of the opinion that  the procedure for grant of operating rights in the  proposed Bill is
considered reasonably flexible.  The Offshore Areas are repository of variety of natural  resources.  In order to exclude
overlapping of granting of operating rights   for exploration and mining of non-petroleum mineral resources   and
petroleum  resources, or for excluding areas rich in fishing     and for excluding areas sensitive  from security and
strategic point of view,  it  is  necessary    that the areas which  would be released for grant of operating rights under the
proposed legislation, are  released periodically in consultation with  all the concerned Departments/Ministries.  In
particular, the procedure for grant of reconnaissance permit is totally flexible, since reconnaissance permit is envisaged
as a non-exclusive permit and   any number of persons could be granted reconnaissance permit over the same area or
even for the same minerals.
9.         The Committee  notes that the offshore areas  would be released periodically for grant  of operating rights for
systematic development of mineral resources of the offshore area.  In order to exclude  overlapping of granting of
operating rights for exploration/mining of non petroleum mineral resources and petroleum resources,   or for excluding 
areas   rich in fishing , the  areas would  be notified for  grant in consultation  with the Ministry of Petroleum  and
Natural Gas, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and the Department of  Animal Husbandry and Dairying. 
Similarly, in order to  ensuing that the areas used  by the Indian Navy, Coast Guard, Indian Space Research
Organisation (ISRO) for exercises/firing  etc. and areas for traffic separation routes, maritime safety routes and the like
are  not notified for grant.  Consultation would be done with the Ministry of Defence before  notifying areas for grant.
10.       Replying to  the Committee's query regarding to  what  extent the proposed  legislation provides  encouragement 
to private sector  in the field of  offshore  areas the Department of Mines stated that   the Bill has been formulated to
provide  a legal  frame  work for entry of private sector in the offshore areas.  The Offshore Areas Mineral (
Development and Regulation ) Bill, 2001 provide equal emphasis on the development and  regulation aspects of
minerals as both aspects are essential.  The Mines and Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957  also has
similar provisions for  ensuring conservation and regulation measures.  Provisions like, power of the  Central
Government to authorize entry, inspection, search and seizure, power to issue directions for conservation and systematic
development of offshore  Minerals, pollution, marine environment, coastal erosion, etc. are essential in the  national
interest and in the interest of mineral  conservation.  The proposed Bill  also  provides  that notwithstanding anything 
contrary contained in the legislation,  if the Central Government is  of the opinion that in the interest of offshore
mineral  development, it is necessary to do so,  it may in any specific case, authorize grant, renewal or transfer of any
operating right to any person on such terms and  conditions as it  may specify in this behalf.  This enabling clause
underlines the  intention of the Central Government that  development of minerals in the offshore areas is its primary
concern.
11.       The Committee observes that  the Offshore Areas Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Bill, 2001 empowers
the Central Government to make rules in case of pollution of offshore   environment and  security and  safety  of  
marine life including fin and  shell fish,  coral and other species.  Sub-clause 2 of  the clause  20 of the proposed Bill 
provides that  every holder of the operating right shall be liable for any pollution or damage to marine environment
resulting from his activities in the offshore areas.  Once the law is enacted, the rules would be framed in consultation
with the Ministries/Departments concerned.
12.       The representatives of  Legislation Department , Ministry of Law, justice and Company Affairs  impressed upon
the Committee that proposed legislation adequately safeguards the national interest in  all respect.      in order to
safeguard defence and security   interests of the  country, the  provisions  of   the  legislation are in  addition to and not
in derogation of any other law for the time being in force in the offshore areas.  Further, the offshore areas would  be
released periodically for grant of operating rights only after inter-Departmental consultations with the 
Ministries/Departments ( including the  Ministry of  Defence)  who  have parallel interest in the offshore areas, and in 
order to  ensure that the areas   used by Indian Navy Coast Guard, etc. for  exercising, the areas for traffic separation
routes,  and maritime safety routes, are not notified.

13.       The Committee   understands that the  under proposed legislation   the reconnaissance permit would be a non-
exclusive permit, any number of persons could be granted reconnaissance permit over the same area or  even for the
same minerals.  Hence the question of determining priority will not arise in cases of grant of reconnaissance permits, nor
will be reconnaissance permit holder have any claim of priority for grant  of an exploration  licence.  No exploration
licence or production lease could be granted to any person over an area unless  he submits a work  programme for   the
exploration operation or development of mineral deposits in that area.  This incorporated to ensure that exploration and
mining operations in the offshore area   are  Government shall not grant an operating right to any person unless  such a
person is an Indian national or a company as defined in Section 3(1)  of the Companies Act, 1956.  Employment of  
foreigners by the operating right holder  shall be subject to separate Government clearance.  Production lease for atomic
minerals would only be granted after consultation with the  Department of Atomic Energy of the Government of India.
14.       The Department of Mines  informed Committee that proposed  legislation  provides for an enabling provision
whereby the Central Government,  by notification in the official gazette, may prescribe   norms for the safety and health
of persons , and safety and security of property in offshore areas. The Department of Mines further  informed
Committee that   proposed legislation shall  have an  enabling  provision for authorising  the framing of detailed rules by
the Central Government in case of pollution of offshore  environment and security and safety of marine life including 
fin and shell fish, coral and  other species.  Every holder of the operating rights shall be liable for any  pollution  or
damage to marine environment resulting from his activities in the offshore areas.
15.       The Department of Mines  impressed on the  Committee that   the opinion/comments of Departments and
Ministries in the Government of India , having stakes  in the offshore areas  were consulted and their  opinion were
sought while discussing and finalising the Bill.   The Department of Mines  had  consulted the Ministries of Defence,
Environment and Forests, External  Affairs, Petroleum and Natural Gas,  Commerce and Industry and  the 
Departments  of    Ocean Development, Atomic  Energy , Animal Husbandry and Dairying, Science and Technology,
Legal Affairs  and the Legislative Department  before formulating the Offshore Areas Mineral ( Development
Regulation)  Bill, 2001.   The process of consultation with the above  Ministries/Departments   has  continued for more
than two years.  There were no difference of opinion, while there have been suggestions for  modifications in the 
drafting of the Bill.  The suggestions given by the different Ministries/Departments have been incorporated in the
proposed Bill.
16.       Justifying  the criterion  for royalty and fixed rent as  indicated  in Schedule -I and Schedule-II of the proposed
legislation the Department of Mines apprised the Committee  that  the working group had felt that the offshore areas
legislation should contain the necessary enabling provision in order to discourage acquisition of   large areas for
speculative purposes.  It had also recommended that  in order to  avoid litigation, the rates of royalty for minerals on
offshore areas may be the   same.  Accordingly the provisions regarding royalty may be made on par with the provisions
in the Mines and Minerals ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.The rates of royalty under section 9 of the Mines
and Minerals ( Development and Regulation ) Act, 1957 have been notified last on 12
th September, 2000 and the rates
of royalty in Offshore Areas Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Bill, 2001 have been indicated at the same level.
Fixed rent  is basically the minimum royalty expected from a lease hold.  Rate of fixed rent for a standard block of 5
minutes by  5 minutes (covering an areas  of approximately 83 sq km. has been based on the  expected minimum
production from a standard block.  The representatives of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and
Company Affairs endorsed  the view points of the Department of Mines.
17.       Having heard the Secretaries,  Department  of Mines and  Legislative  Department, Ministry of  Law  Justice and
Company  Affairs and the  clarifications given by them to the various queries and having considered the  papers
furnished by the Ministry, the Committee agrees with the proposal of the  Department of Mines that   the proposed bill 
rightly  intends to provide for  development and regulation  of mineral resources in the  territorial waters continental
shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India and to provide for matters connected therewith or
incidental thereto.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Relat ed Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been author ised by the Committee to present on its beha lf, present this 
Seventh Report of the Committee on the working of Bharat Gold Minies Limited which falls 
under the jurisdiction of Ministry of Mines. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 15th June, 1993 identified 'Bharat Gold Mines' as 
one of subjects for indepth study and report. The Committee directe d the Secretariat to obta in 
a detailed Background Note on the subject from the Ministry of Mines. 
3. At its sitting held on 28th June, 1993 the Committee held a general discussion on the 
note furnished by the Ministry on the subject and finalised a questionnaire for furth er 
clarificatiOns by the Ministry. 
4. The Committee also heard the oral ev1aence of the Secretary of the Ministry alongwith 
the representat ives of Bharat Gold Mines Limited at its two meetings held on 30th September 
and lOth November, 1993 respectively for clarifications. 
5. The Committee at its meeting held on the 9th November, 1993 also heard the oral 
evidence of the representatives of the Workers' Unions operating at Bha rat Gold Mines Limited 
witl;l a view to eliciting their views on the functioning of the company. 
6. In its meeting held on 11th November, 1993 the Committee decided to constitute a Sub­
Committee to visit Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka for an on the spot study of the working in 
Bharat Gold Mines Limited . The Chairman of the Committee accordingly constituted a Sub­
Committee of the following Member s for the purpose. 
1. Shrimati Suseela Gopalan - Convenor 
2. Shri J.P. Javali 
3. Shri K. K. Veerappan 
4. Shri K. H. Muniyappa 
5. Shri V. Dhananjaya Kumar 
6. Shri Tej Nar<tyan Singh 
7. Shri P.G. Narayanan 
7. The Sub-Committe e visited the Kolar Gold Fields on 5th and 6th January, 1994. The 
Sub-Committee heard the oral evidences of the repre sentatives of the worke rs unions operating 
at Kolar Gold Fields and also the representatives of Bharat Gold Mines Limited Management 
and the Ministry of Mines. The Sub-Committee submitted a study report on its visit. The study 
report was considered by the Committee at its meeting held on 22nd Febr uary, 1994. After 
some discussion the Committee unanimously adopted the report submitted by the Sub­
Committee. 
8. The Committee at its meeting held on 23rd February, 1994 heard and considered the 
views of Shri S. Natarajan on the subject as recommend ed by the Sub-Committee. 
9. The Committee considered the subject in 11 sittings and ado pted the draft report at its 
meeting held on 30th March , 1994. 
10. The study report of the Sub-Committee is annexed (Annexure 1). 
11. On the basis of the documents furnished by the Ministry of Mines, the oral evidence of 
the representatives of the Ministry, workers unions management of Bharat Gold Mines and the 

study VISit of the Sub-Committee to Kolar Gold Fields as stated above the Committee 
recommends that:-
11.1 It is necessary to allay the fear of imminent closure of BGML at Kolar which is 
looming large on the workers and their families and other inhabitants of the area. 
They are living under a fear psychosis as the sword of closure is hanging over their 
heads. To remove this fear psychosis it is necessary to declare in unequivocal terms 
that the Company will not be allowed to close down and every effort will be made to 
revive it at the apex nation,al level. 
11.2 The Company has been referred to BIFR. Now it can not take any action for the 
revival without the prior permission of BIFR. Hence it is necessary that the reference 
of BGML, Kolar to BIFR be revoked forthwith and taken out from the purview of 
BIFR. 
11.3 To bring the company on rails· requisite funds should be given to establish a plant for 
recycling the huge stock of tailing so as to extract gold therefrom. The Committee 
observes that once the plant is established and it starts running within two to three 
years not only the company will wipe out its losses but it will also start earning 
profits. To boost the morale of the company the Ministry of Mines must come 
forward. The Government may either make available 41 crores of rupees as 
Budgetary support or soft loan to the company or stand as a gurantor to enable the 
company to get loans from banks and financial institutions. The management can also 
explore the possibility of hypothecating its surplus land to raise the funds for the 
plant of course with the prior approval of the Government. 
11.4 The management can raise the requisite funds for its revivial by selling its surplus 
land at the existing market rates as the land can fetch good prices but this step should 
be resorted to as the last step because the land can be utilised for agricultural 
pruposes particularly the cashew growing. Presently the management has planted 
eucliptus in parts of the surplus land and expecting to get some revenue therefrom 
but keeping in view that this variety makes the land infertile its plantation may be 
discouraged. 
11.5 The Security network of the company should be streamlined and every effort should 
be made to prevent pilferage of gold produced by the company. Frisking be mae 
compulsory for everyone coming out of the premises where gold is produced 
irrespective of his status. The Security personnel be provided modern gadgets to 
detect pilferage of gold. A vigilance wing should also be established to keep overall 
watch over the movements in the premises including that of security personnel. 
Surprise checks should be conducted and activities of the goldsmiths living around 
Kolar be monitored to prevent passing of pilfered gold. 
11.6 Survey of the gold deposits in the area should be counducted in more and more 
scientific way. BGML is presently wholly dependent on Geological Survey of India 
for this purpose. The management may have its own team to do this job. Technology 
from other countries like South Africa and Australia can be obtained in this field as 
they have the latest know-how in this area. South Africa in particular have the 
resembling conditions as that of Kolar and doing very well. Their co-operation can be 
more helpful. 
Technology from countries like South Africa, Australia etc. can be explored who can help in 
modernising the existing techniques of BGML on profit sharing basis. 
11.7 The BGML is undertaking diversification activities to earn more revenue. It is 

manufacturing mmmg equipments and also providing mmmg consultancy services. 
The Government can help BGML by securing orders from other departments. Export 
possibilities should also be explored. The diversification activities should be encour­
aged to create more job opportunities. 
11.8 BGML being a Government of India enterprise it is the onus of the Government to 
provide funds for the modernisation of the mills and mining techniques of the 
company. The funds may be in the form of long term loans with reasonable interest 
thereon. Since it is the only one establishment engaged in production of precious 
yellow metal in the country phasing out is not advisable at all. If proper investments 
are made in this company and new era of hopes and dedication is generated the 
company can run smoothly for the next fifty to sixty years. But there must be a will 
on the part of the Government to run this company. 
11.9 The BGML is spending a substantial portion of its earnings on power tariff. 
Understandably the Karnataka Electricity Board had established a power house 
exclusively for BGML. The production cost pe~; unit in that power house comes to few 
paise but the Board is charging exorbitant tariff from BGML. The State Electricity 
Board should be apprised of the gravity of the situation and persuaded to reduce the 
power tariff to reduce the burden of BGML. Similarly the State Government is 
charging royalty from BGML without extending any facility. The State can also be 
persuaded to forgo charging royalty from BGML. 
12. The ·Committee has come to conclusion that the past performance of the present 
management has· been quite dismal and the change of the management could be a better future of 
the company. 
13. The Committee is of the opinion that i( the above mentioned steps are take n by the 
Government and BGML there is every possibility of the revival of BGML and certainly it will 
prove to be a national asset. · 
14. The Committer~. trusts that its observations and recom·mendations as mentioned above 
will receive serious consideration for implementation.

GOLD PRICE FORMULA 
The Sub-Committee has gathered that till the formation of the company the gold was bought 
by the Government at IMF prices. In April, 1974. the pricing policy underwent a change and the 
old was to be sold at London Metal Exchange Rates The pricing policy further underwent a 
change during 1976-88 as per details given below:-
(i) The subsidy payable is equal to the difference between the IMF Price (Rs. 84.40 per 10 
grams) and the cost of production of 10 grams of gold in 1975-76 plus 12% on capital 
and reserves. 
(ii) Government could review from time to time the cost of produ ction and take into 
account any inescapable increase in cost of production. 
(iii) This price was subject to a minimum of the average international price in the prccedmg 
month and a maximum of the average international price in the rrc ceding month plus 
25%. 
(iv) The Government of India from November, 1982 fom1ulatcd the following formula: 
"Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) and .Butti Gold Mines Limited (HGML) each 
be allowed to meet half of the total industrial demand for gold at the prevailing 
domestic price. The production of BGML and HGML over and above this quantity as 
well as the ehtire production of Hindustan Copper Limited would be taken over by the 
Mint at an average international price during the preceding month plus 12.1/2% or the 
average domestic price during the preceding month whichever is lower.·· 
(v) From 1.4.1984, the pricing policy of Government for BGML gold was LMc price 35% 
or Indian Market rate whichever is lower.

(f) Survey of the gold deposits in the area should be conducted in more and more scientific 

way. BGML is presently wholly dependent on Geological Survey of India for this 
purpose. The management may have its own team to do this job . From other countrie s 
like South Africa and Australi a can be obtained in this field as they have the latest know 
how in this area. South Africa in particular have the resembling conditions as that of 
Kolar and doing very well. Their Co-operat ion can be more helpful. 
(g) Technology from countries like South Africa, Australia etc. can be explored who can 
help in modernising the existing technique s of BGML on profit sharing basis. 
(h) The BGML is undertaking diversification activities to earn more revenue. It is 
manufacturing mining equipments and also providing mining· Consultancy services. The 
Government can help BGML by securing orders from other departments. Export 
possibilities should also be explored. The diversification activities should be encouraged 
to create more job opportunities. 
(i) BGML being a Government of India enterprise it is the onus of the Government to 
provide funds for the moderni satio n of the mills and mining techniques of the company. 
The funds may be in the form of long term loans with reasonable interest. thereon. Since 
it is the only one establishment engaged in proauction of precious yellow metal in the 
country phasing out is not advisable at all. If proper investments are made in this 
company and new era of hopes and dedication is generated the company can run 
smoothly for the next fifty to sixty years. But there must be a will on the part of the 
Government to run this company. 
(j) The BGML is spending a substantial portion of its earnings on power tariff. Understand­
ably · the Karnataka Electricity Board had established a power house exclusively for 
BGML. The production cost per unit in that power house comes to few paise but the 
Board is charging exorbitant tariff from BGML. The STate Electricity Board should be 
apprised of the gravity of the situation and persuaded to reduce the power tariff to 
reduce the burden of BGML. Similarly the State Government is charging royalty from 
BGML without extendi.ng any facility. The State can also be persuaded to forgo charging 
royalty from BGML. 
The Sub-Committee has come to the conclusion that the past performance of the 
present management has been quite dismal and the change of the management, as a test 
case, could be a better future of the company. 
The Sub-Committee is of the opinion that if the above mentioned steps are taken by 
the Government and BGML there is every possibility of the revival of BGML and 
certainly it will prove to be a national asset. 
The Committee may consider. 
CONVENOR.

REPORT
1.         History  is a witness to the fact  that  minerals  have  been the  basis of classification of human  civilization.   A
civilization undertakes development  in consonance with a pattern of physical  endowment of valuable minerals like Copper,
Iron Ore,  Aluminium,  Zinc, Lead, Gold,   Cobalt, Manganese, Graphite, Lime Stone, platinum etc.    Since minerals resources
are wealth hidden   beneath the earth-curst and are wasting assets    their conservation and planned   exploitation is of
paramount importance to  national economic development and growth .  As a matter of fact,  mineral resources not only provide
the basic inputs to domestic industry,  but also account for sizeable export and foreign exchange earnings.  Henceforth, the
development and regulation of the mineral sector is concomitant to the optimal utilisation of resources which ensures all round
development and growth of national economy.
1.1.      The Department of   Mines is  responsible for development and regulation of the mineral sector including  the mining
and metallurgy     of all non-ferrous metals both in private and public  sectors, but excluding   natural Gas, Petroleum, Coal and
Atomic   minerals.  As per the Annual Report (2001-02) of   the Department of Mines  has been   allotted subjects  as under:-
Legislation for regulation  of mines and development  of    minerals within the territory of  India, including   mines    and
minerals  underlying the ocean within the territorial waters  or the continental shelf, or the Exclusive Economic zone and other
Maritime Zones of  India as may be specified from time to  time by or under any law made by Parliament.
Regulation  of mines and development of minerals   other than coal,  lignite and sand  for  stowing and any minerals declared as
prescribed substances for the  purposes  of the  Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (33 of 1962)  under the control of the Union as
declared by law,   including   questions concerning  regulation and development of minerals in various states and the matter
connected therewith with or incidental thereto.
All other metals and minerals not  specifically allotted to any  other Ministry/ Department  such as aluminium, zinc , copper,
gold, diamond and nickel.
Planning development and control of  and assistance to all industries dealt with by the Department.
At the Secretariat level  the  Department of Mines is  mainly engaged in direction, supervision and coordination of five
divisions which inter-alia include Survey and Exploration,  Mines, Metal, General Administration and Finance and Accounts
Division.   Survey and Exploration has two principle agencies i.e. Geological Survey of India (GSI) and Mineral Exploration
Corporation Ltd. (MECL) for the implementation of the programmes of this division while Mines Division has one  subordinate
office to implement the programmes of the division, viz. Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM). Metal division of the Department of
Mines deals with the planning, exploration, development, monitoring of programmes and research in respect of non-ferrous
metals both in the public and private sectors General Administration Division is mainly concerned with the establishment and
administrative matter of the Department and Finance and Accounts Division is concerned with the budget, financial scrutiny of
projects and other proposals, rendering financial advice and maintenance and compilation of accounts.
Department of Mines has two  subordinate offices, namely :-
Geological  Survey of India ( HQ Kolkata)
Indian Bureau of Mines (HQ Nagpur)
Public Sectors Undertakings (PSUs) - Department of Mines  has four   PSUs
National Aluminium Company Ltd.  (NALCO), Bhubaneshwar
Hindustan Copper Ltd. (HCL), Kolkata
Minerals Exploration Corporation Ltd. (MECL).
Bharat Gold Mines Ltd.  (BGML). (closed since  1
st March, 2001)
1.5.      Joint Venture Undertakings ;  There are  three companies in which the Department of Mines held equity shareholding
during  2001-02
Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. (BALCO), New  Delhi. ( a company jointly owned by Sterlite Industries Ltd. and
Government of India)
Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL).  ( a company jointly owned by Sterlite Industries Ltd. and Government of India)
Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) ( a company jointly owned by the State  Government of Sikkim and the Government of
India).  The  allocation of business relating to Sikkim Mining Corporation  (SMC) has been transferred  to the Department of
Development of North  Eastern Region on 21.12.2001.
1.6.      Research Institutions; There are three Research Institutions under the Department of  Mines, namely:

National Institute  of Miners' health, Kolar  Gold Fields, Karnataka.
